utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm told you have something to raise, Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. I have spoken further with the government of the United Kingdom and they have indicated that so long as the documents that are being entered into evidence here by either the Prosecution or by the Defence, so long as they are the redacted versions as redacted by the United Kingdom they do not need to go under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What in general do the redaction relate to.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Privileged information, confidential information. There's redactions to people who were receiving at the United Kingdom, that type of thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So essentially the content of the documents would be public.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Largely, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That is excellent and thank you for dealing with that so quickly. We'll now go into closed is session to allow the witness to enter the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sure you'll recollect, Mr. Crosland, being reminded when you were here before that the solemn declaration you made at the outset of your evidence to speak the truth will continue to apply to that evidence until it's completed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan, the order of cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. We will follow the indictment with one change. General Lazarevic will precede General Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You have questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yesterday, you testified about your visit to Glodjane, and you also talk about that in your statement P2645 at paragraph 41, and you say that you were taken under MUP escort to the village of Glodjane where you witnessed six to eight bodies. You were told that they were Serbs allegedly killed by the KLA, but you add that you were not sure, it was impossible to tell who the victims were at the time. I'd like to ask you some further questions about that. The location you were taken to was the canal leading to Lake Radonjic which is near the village of Glodjane; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And it would be fair to say, I think, that you had been brought there, there had been no investigation conducted, and it was impossible to tell who the victims were just by looking. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's an entirely fair statement, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Sir, I've received a p copy of a statement you gave to the Prosecutor in June 2006. It's a statement you gave in connection with the Haradinaj case, and in that statement you told the Prosecutor that on that day you toured the site at Radonjic Lake and you noticed that there were ten to 15 splash marks of gunshots on the wall of the canal; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were a number of gunshots, yes, on the canal, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And you collected six to 12 empty cases of Chinese ammunition close to the bodies. You brought these cases back to the UK for analysis, and the forensic people in the UK confirmed that the ammunition was of Chinese origin; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I understand, it's correct, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And this was an indication that the KLA was responsible for the killings because the KLA used Chinese munitions and the Serbs did not. You knew that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's, if I may say so with respect, sir, a generalisation in that ammunition could have been placed there. It -- what you are saying is correct, that in general the KLA, as far as we understand, did use Chinese ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: All right. And you also told the Prosecutor, in this statement, that the canal where the bodies were found was about one kilometre from the headquarters of Ramush Haradinaj and that he was the undisputed KLA commander of the area, and you said the crime scene was in his backyard. That's how you put it; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And during this interview you were informed by the Prosecutor that Mr. Haradinaj had been indicted for the events that you saw at Radonjic Lake; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you say so, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And then in paragraph 30 of this statement, you say you met Mr. Haradinaj three to four times at his headquarters. That's correct, isn't?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And you were also told by the Prosecutor that the indictment against Mr. Haradinaj included approximately 39 victims, and you were -- you know that -- you were told that the victims included Serbs, Albanians of Islam-- Islamic faith and Catholic faith and non-Serbs and non-Albanians from Kosovo; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We encountered various persons who had been shot and dumped by the road. Their exact origins would be very difficult to -- for me to testify to under -- under oath.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: But you knew the KLA did in fact execute Serbs and Albanians and other people who lived in Kosovo of other ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the intelligence that we understood, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: At paragraph 27, you say this: "From my experience on the ground, it is clear to me that Ramush and his brother were involved in criminal activities, fuel, cigarettes, prostitution, racketeering, et cetera. I am sure Ramush is up to his neck in it even to this day." This is information you provided; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And at paragraph 28, again, you say: "In the area that Ramush controlled, there were well-tried smuggling routes date being back to the Ottoman times. The same routes were used by the KLA to smuggle weapons and other goods. Pec, for example, was well known for its various nefarious activities during the war partly because it was so close to Montenegro." Now, this is information you provided also; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Then you told the Prosecutor this at paragraph 21: When you were asked whether anybody confronted Mr. Haradinaj with the killings at the canal leading to Radonjic Lake, you said, and I quote: "I think that a conscious decision had been made to support the KLA, and then as a result the difficult questions were not asked. Perhaps for this reason I am not aware of anyone from the international community asking Ramush tough questions about the bodies found in the canal leading to the Radonjic Lake. "I never did, even though I met him on several occasions. It was clear in those days that Ramush and his brother Daut were the future main players in this area. They were clearly the bosses of the Pec, Prizren, Decan, Djakovica area. The international community wanted to keep them on side, not alienate them or tarnish their reputation." That's what you told the Prosecutor; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, sir and I think that has appeared to be the case so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: At paragraph 25, you said this: "The international community supported the KLA and they knew that. Bill Clinton, Richard Holbrooke, Madeleine Albright had decided that there was going to be regime change in Serbia and the KLA was one of the tools to make this happen. From that point on, whatever reservations I or others may have had against the KLA was not relevant. The position of the -- the position the international community took at Rambouillet in 1999 was consistent with that policy." This again is what you told the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And when you completed this interview in June 2006, after you reviewed the statement and initialed every page, you signed and dated an acknowledgement stating that the statement was true, to the best of your knowledge and recollection. You gave the statement voluntarily and you knew it may be used in proceedings in this Tribunal; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. O'Sullivan. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Crosland, my name is Toma Fila and I'm Defence counsel for Mr. Sainovic. Good morning and I won't take up too much of your time. I would like us to deal with something first and foremost that someone -- that no one has dealt with before as far as your statement is concerned. I'm referring to the Milosevic-Holbrooke Agreement. If you have your statement, this is paragraphs 61 through 64.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Right. In your report, you stated that you -- or, rather, in your telegram of the 2nd of October, you said that the MUP and the army of Yugoslavia ceased all activity, that there are signs of troop withdrawal, and that this is when Milosevic and Holbrooke were negotiating. Now, you said that the formal agreement between Milosevic and Holbrooke, and that is what is stated in your statement on the 28th and 29th of October, that is not correct. That is not when the agreement was actually reached. It was earlier. It was the 13th or 14th of October. Do you allow for that possibility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If that is -- excuse me, sir, if that is what is in the statement then, yes. I don't have the statement in front of me, so I can't argue with your supposition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, the -- the statement says the formal agreement followed. That's after the Holbrooke-Milosevic talks with 28th and 29th October specified for the withdrawal of forces. I don't think it's being said to be the date of the agreement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- I physically supervised the withdrawal.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The agreement concluded on the 28th, 29th of October. That is what it says here. Well, never mind. That is not the reason why I'm putting this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think there's a language problem because the English -- the English version of the statement, which is its original, says the 28th and 29th were the dates specified for the withdrawal of forces. Now, do you know the actual date on which Milosevic and Holbrooke reached agreement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not certain, Your Honour. All I can say is I was physically on the ground when the three battle groups concerned moved back to barracks, and I then reported that both back to the Ministry of Defence and to the Supreme Allied Commander in Europe, General Wesley Clark. What date that was, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: As far as we can tell, this fundamental agreement doesn't appear to exist in black and white.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Nobody has been able to find a copy of it. There are summaries in press statements, but we haven't seen the agreement itself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry. Forgive me, sir. All I was doing was -- or overseeing the physical withdrawal of the three battle groups, and I then sent that required message to the authorities and stated. At the same time and to the credit of the Serbs, three other MUP were then killed virtually in front of me, so the VJ did what -- and the MUP did what they were asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. President, that is precisely the reason why I put the question. I hope that the translation is not wrong yet, again. In paragraph 63, you say when the Holbrooke Agreement was signed in 1998. So because of the letter that you sent me, I conducted an investigation to Belgrade to see whether there was ever an agreement in writing, I emphasise in writing. I talked to the Prime Minister who is going to testify here with the Foreign Minister with all the Socialist Party witnesses. I don't want the Prosecutor to hold this against me. I'm not taking the stand myself. Everybody said that Milosevic showed a little piece of paper with his own handwriting - Milosevic's handwriting, that is - that he dictated to Prime Minister Marjanovic 11 points, and that is what I consider to be the agreement until you warned me. So the point is that this was never signed. A written agreement was never signed. This is why I put this question to the gentleman, and I'm not going to deal it any more and let's move on again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's probably saved you bringing four witnesses here, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you. Now I'll deal with something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now I'd like to draw your attention to your statement again, paragraph 47. You said there that you assume you are not making any claims, but you assume that there was a coordination centre presumably in Pristina in order to avoid friendly fire or blue-on-blue, as you had put it. In response to Ms. Carter's questions, you said that there should be at least two parties involved there. I assume that you meant the army and the police, and you also refer to some politicians. Before I put a question to you, I would like to ask you that -- to tell you, rather, that General Klaus Naumann, you know who that is, testified here on the 14th of December, 2006. And on page 91367, lines 10 through 23, he said that from his own intelligence sources, NATO, that is, he had the knowledge that there was a coordination centre in Nis and in Belgrade. Do you allow for that possibility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, I -- I would be very surprised if there was not an alternative communications centre at the heart of 3rd Army in Nis and a further one in Belgrade for the day-to-day handling of the political level of what was a very serious incident. So it doesn't surprise me at all, sir, no. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So don't you find it logical that politicians would be sitting in Belgrade and resolving these questions, as you saw from one of the documents that the Prosecutor showed you? Don't you think that would be logical, rather than in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, with respect, I think that was -- I was indicating, yesterday, you had political persons in Pristina throughout this incident, and I suspect that those local politicians of considerable weight would also be involved in a coordination centre which, would be linked to the headquarters of 3rd Army in Nis as also to the headquarters in Beograd. So I'm delighted to hear it. I don't find it strange. I would welcome that political control over the military forces, which is hopefully more or less standard procedure across the civilised world.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now I would like to deal with a third group of questions, my last one. In several statements, you said that you were in Kosovo many times from 1996 onwards and in Belgrade, and that you never met Nikola Sainovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I'm aware, sir, I never met him. I may have -- he may have been present at one of the many functions that defence attaches were asked to come to.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you know perhaps that Mr. Sainovic, in the government of Yugoslavia, was in charge of foreign policy from 1996,; that is to say, the implementation of the Dayton agreement onwards and that then Kosovo came under that? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't know that at the time, sir, no. I mean, I was -- as a defence attache, I'm accredited to the Vojska Jugoslavija, not to the MUP. So we had very little dealings with the MUP and all the personalities within the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Nikola Sainovic is not a person from the MUP. He's a person from the government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia; whereas, the MUP is the MUP of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is very correct, sir. I, as a defence attache, am accredited direct to then the Chief of the General Staff, General Perisic, and to the Vojska Jugoslavija, full stop, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In your role, though, would you not normally be aware of who -- who was the Minister responsible for the Department of Foreign Affairs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We were briefed on that, Your Honour. The -- the gentleman just asked me a question. I don't recall at the time, it's nearly 10 years ago now, who was exactly in which position, as these positions did actually change quite frequently. But I obviously, as part of the my brief, sir, I would attempt to keep up-to-date with the key personalities, and I apologize if Mr. Sainovic was the Foreign Minister. My mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it may be important, because the point is being put to you that he was in that role from 1996, and therefore we might draw some conclusions about how prominent he was depending on your knowledge of that fact because you were there from 1997.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was there from September 1996, sir, till 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your permission, Nikola Sainovic was not Minister of Foreign Affairs. Zivorad Jovanovic was Minister of Foreign Affairs. He was deputy federal Prime Minister under Bulatovic's authority, and Bulatovic will testify here. He was in charge of the foreign policy of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia as deputy Prime Minister. But all right, I would like --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Help me on that, Mr. Fila. You're quite right as Judge Kamenova was pointing out to me. He wasn't the Minister of Foreign Affairs. But the way you put the question was that he was in charge of foreign policy. Does that mean that the Minister of Foreign Affairs was answerable to Mr. Sainovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. They were all answerable to Prime Minister Momir Bulatovic. But relations with foreign diplomats were of particular significance because the implementation of Dayton, Your Honour, was very important. It had to do with Bosnia, partly Croatia as well and then it went further on. Quite simply the volume of the work involved was big.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And there were five deputy Prime Ministers in the government, not only one, five. But all right. Could we have 2D8 on the screen, please, the English version, of course, so that the witness can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can you please have a look at this document, and you'll see that Mr. Nikola Sainovic was the chairman of the Commission for Cooperation with the OSCE. This is the Serbian version. It would be better to have the English version displayed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We also have the English one now, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can you see it, Mr. Crosland?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can one infer on the basis of this that he was put in that position because he was in charge of foreign policy with regard to Kosovo, and the OSCE was actually in charge of that particular segment of foreign policy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't -- I don't dispute that. I mean, I came into -- I had very little to do with the OSCE mission, as such. We briefed them when they first arrived, the Kosovo Verification Mission, and then it was a separate entity with all these gentlemen, as you've laid out there in paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right. Yes. Fine. Now I would like to deal with P683. This is a telegram that you sent, Mr. Crosland, in relation to the meetings held on the 3rd of October. That is when you received General Dimitrijevic. However, what I'm interested in is paragraph 10. Let me jog your memory. You say that it was your idea to have an ambassadorial meeting held; that is to say, between Her Majesty's ambassador and Perisic and Sainovic, and they were not there and Bugarcic came instead of Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, can you back to the -- could you go back to the top, because I'm not certain whether this was a telegram or a telegram sent from me as a Brit mil attache. If it's a diplomatic telegram --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Bugarcic. It is paragraph 10 of your telegram.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The witness wants to see the beginning of the telegram, Mr. Fila, so he can identify the document to his own satisfaction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This -- with great respect, sir, this document has been sent by the ambassador and not by myself. My -- my telegrams where I -- the telegrams that I sent were Brit mil attache.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I thought it was your telegram. I apologise, but nevertheless you attended that meeting. So I wanted to ask you about that. Could you please just look at paragraph 10. And I do apologise to you because I did believe that it was your telegram. So could we please have paragraph 10 displayed. Right. At the very bottom down here. Could you just lift it up a bit, please, the text. Have you read it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I read it, sir, yeah, but it's only half of the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, it continues. Could we please see the next page of the English version.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've read the paragraph, sir. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now I would like you to comment on something. You see that Bugarcic is informing his excellency the ambassador of the United Kingdom and you, both of you being present there, to the effect that Sainovic confirms what Andjelkovic had said, and that that is an official statement made by the government regarding their obligation of civil reconstruction; that is to say, to rebuild what had been destroyed. And the second thing they are informing you about is that six battle groups had returned to barracks and so on and so forth. My question is the following: Is that not what a deputy Prime Minister should do, a person who is politically in charge of Kosovo, that he should inform your ambassador who should in turn inform your government as to what was going on? Don't you think that this is a political move made by a politician? Is that not his duty? Is that not his obligation, If you agree with what I'm saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, with great respect, I've said in my statement that there were occasions when pressure was applied to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia that troop reductions were made throughout the province of Kosovo. I'm afraid to say that these lasted for some couple of weeks and then --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I'm sorry that's not my question. That's not my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: My question, Mr. Crosland, is how do you interpret the fact that Sainovic is conveying the decision of the government of Serbia to rebuild what had been destroyed? Is that not the right kind of gesture to be made by a man who is in charge of foreign policy, to inform the ambassador of another country as to what was going on? I'm not asking you about troop withdrawal. I'm asking you about what Mr. Sainovic did. Is that not the kind of thing a politician would do? Is that not the impression that you had had? I don't know whether you understand what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, with great respect, when I left Kosovo on the 18th of March, 1999 for the last time, there had been no rebuilding of any kind at all. There was continued excessive damage caused to Kosovo Albanian housing throughout the whole province of Kosovo. Those, sir, are the facts. They are documented in several of my reports and several other personnel have seen them. So I can't accept Mr. Sainovic may --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: That is not what I asked you. You're not responding to my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Try to leave out of account whether the information was accurate or inaccurate, and try to confine your answer to the essence of this question which is, in fact, assume for the moment the information's accurate, is that the sort of thing you would expect a politician to be doing, to be conveying this sort of detail to your ambassador?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. Well, one would. The fact of the matter is that nothing was rebuilt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's quite Sir, I understand, but there's no need to be quite so defensive on that point, because we do understand the distinction between what's said and what's actually done.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And, therefore, we must try to separate these. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just have a look. I don't think I'll have any more questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Finally, you left Kosovo and Yugoslavia, in general, on the very eve of the bombing, roughly when the mission left, too; is that right? And then you returned when NATO came in or, rather, when the UN came in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, we left Belgrade on the night before the bombing, and then I returned as a liaison officer for the NATO Rapid Reaction Corps when we came back into Kosovo; and then subsequent to that in 2000, I came back to reopen our embassy.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right. So your information ends on that day, on the eve of the bombing. I want to ask you whether you know what the positions of Yugoslav politicians were during the bombing itself. Do you have information of that kind? Yes or no? During the state of war, that is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have information of that kind, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And what is that information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was working within our Ministry of Defence, which is quite natural because I'd been the last person within Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and advising on how the -- the situation should go forward, which is extremely difficult situation. And I was attempting, if you really want to know, to put the Yugoslav position to our government and to those who would listen, and I have no problem in telling you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Very well. That is what I had to add to Mr. O'Sullivan's questions. And now I would like to ask you something else. Twice you talked to Mr. Philip Coo in 2006 and earlier on, was it? Can I ask you in what capacity he talked to you the first time and the second time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, I think -- I think it's about the fifth time that I have of attended this court and I've given many, many interviews. So, with great respect, sir, it was during one of the investigations that I was asked for my views. I think one of the times I met Mr. Coo, and Ms. Carter will tell me otherwise, was in preparation for this particular trial and one, I think, was in preparation for Ramush Haradinaj, I think. But, as I say, I've given many interviews in -- for the benefit of this court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The question, Mr. Crosland, is in what capacity Mr. Coo was speaking to you. Do you know what his role was when he interviewed you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I understand, Your Honour, he was one of the investigators for the ICTY, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. That would be the end of my questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Good morning, Colonel Crosland?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I'm Norman Sepenuk, and I'm an attorney for General Ojdanic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I want to spend a little bit of time talking about your prior statements and testimony concerning Lord Ashdown. We do know from Prosecution Exhibit 2645, that's your statement of October 31 2006, a statement which you swore was true to the best of your knowledge and recollection. And you said at paragraph 51, page 11, and I am quoting now, sir: "On September 26, 27, 1998, Lord Ashdown and I showed Ojdanic photographic evidence of the VJ shelling Suva Reka on 27 August 1998. His reaction was that force would be met with appropriate force." Correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With -- with great respect, sir, I think we covered this yesterday, and there appears to be a date problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. Well --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I recall, and with the best of intentions and under oath, I did not show Lord Ashdown this and that statement, as we went through yesterday, is incorrect. And I think, Your Honour, we went through this, yesterday, so we're back into the same maelstrom of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It sounds though, Mr. Crosland, that Mr. Sepenuk may be wishing to explore why that happened; and if he does, then that's a legitimate thing for him to do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So bear with the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel, and thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And then about six years earlier, Colonel, on December 7, 2000, you submitted a statement to the Prosecutor, which you swore was true to the best of your knowledge and recollection, to the same effect - this is six years earlier - where you said, . "On 26, 27 September 1998, the leader of the UK democratic party, the Right Honourable Paddy Ashdown, and I showed Ojdanic photographic evidence of the VJ shelling Suva Reka on 27 August 1998. His reaction was the categorical denial of the use of the VJ air force and that force would be met with appropriate force." That's 3D508. That's the exhibit, paragraph 5, page 3, and you recall that do you not, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you say so, sir, that is correct. It's a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But the -- I don't understand this business about "air."

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Well, that's what you said in the statement. You might not understand it, but that's what you said in the statement says, "the denial of the use of the VJ air force and that force would be met with appropriate force." That's a direct quote from your statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I don't see the paragraph concerned, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: 3D508. Could we put that up, please? We're talking now about your statement of 7 December 2000. Paragraph 5, page 3.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I still haven't got it, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Can we -- paragraph 5, page 3. 3D508. There we go. You see that, sir, at the top? His reaction was "the categorical denial of the use of the VJ air force and that force would be met with appropriate force you." You --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I never claimed that the VJ air force was being involved in any activities in Kosovo. If fact, I saw, on some occasions, MiG 21s flying out of -- out of Pristina, and there was one occasion I saw a helicopter. And that, during the entire time, was the extent of Vojska Jugoslavija air force in Kosovo. So I don't -- I don't understand. You know, his reaction was a "categorical denial the use of the VJ air force." I never stated that the VJ air force had been used in defensive operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: But you do not deny that appears in a statement, which you swore to be true to the best of your knowledge and belief.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're actually correct, sir. That's an oversight on my behalf, but I'm stating here that I never stated that the VJ air force was used in an aggressive role.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So how that crept in, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And then in the -- in the Milosevic trial, you testified to this effect, looking now at 3D505. Transcript 7938, you were being questioned by the Prosecutor Mr. Ryneveld, and the question was: "Did you also take any video or photographic evidence of what you had seen," and he was referring to a tour that you had taken with Lord Ashdown in late September 1998. You remember the tour with Lord Ashdown, don't you sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do indeed, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And in answer to that question, whether you took any video or photographic evidence at that time, your answer was,"Yes. We did sir, yes." And the question was then put, "And later on did you have a meeting with General Ojdanic in the presence of Lord Ashdown?" Answer: "I believe we did sir, yes." Now, we now know that that testimony was not true; correct sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, yes. And I've stated that yesterday that I believe the dates between August and September have been muddled up in these huge amount of documents. I apologise for that. It's not an intension to mislead the court at all. I just believe it's a misrepresentation of the dates concerned, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Well, when you testified in the Milosevic trial, this muddling up of paragraphs 50 and 51, that wasn't involved, was it? You just flat out testified. That wasn't a statement; that was testimony. So what -- there was nothing muddled up, was there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With respect, sir, I've said I've been asked to testify here on many occasions, and I think there should be some leniency for dates being muddled up. It's not intentional, and I don't intend to mislead the Court, far from it. I think over the 70-odd reports that I have produced for this ICTY, which have given a huge background to the whole situation, that a little bit of leniency should be allowed in an attempt to represent in a very fair and positive manner both sides of this very difficult situation. I have supported the Vojska Jugoslavija, and I've also made it clear, as I've stated in this Court, that they were facing a growing internal counter-insurgency operation. So I don't think I can be accused of being against the Vojska Jugoslavija.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not accusing you of anything, believe me. All I am saying is that that testimony you gave in the Milosevic trial, that you had a meeting with General Ojdanic in the presence of Lord Ashdown was not correct, that's all. And that's so, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This appears to be correct, and I stated that this is one of the areas that appears to be muddled up. I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. And then you came to The Hague to testify in this case, and by the way when did you get here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On which occasion, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Well, we had a supplemental information sheet of information you supplied to Ms. Carter on February 6 2006. Did you -- is that when you got here to prepare your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: 2007. Actually, this says 2006. I will -- I never blame myself, Colonel, for anything. I'm blaming Ms. Carter for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Having got a wife and three daughters, sir, I know exactly where I stand. I believe I arrived on Monday this week, sir. Whatever date that is, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: That's the 5th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're absolutely correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And did you meet with Ms. Carter on the 5th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think -- I think not. I think we met on the 6th, because I didn't arrive here until quite late on the 5th.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Now, when you came here, am I correct in assuming that you were going to testify here pretty much as you had stated in your prior statements of the year 2000, October 2006, and at the Milosevic trial. You were ready to testify that you and Lord Ashdown had shown General Ojdanic photographic evidence of the shelling of Suva Reka on August 27, 1998. Is it fair that you were prepared to so testify before you met with Ms. Carter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, no, that is not actually correct. Because I was approached by Lord Ashdown and my farmer ambassador over this very question, because Lord Ashdown was unhappy that the dates did not tie up with his remembrance of these events. When I got here, I spoke to Ms. Carter and the specific paragraphs were 50 and 51, which we went through in some detail yesterday. Because I said these paragraphs are not, not correct. Now, I apologise that previous statements have been allowed to go forward that stated that I showed this with Lord Ashdown to General Ojdanic. That is not correct. I can only apologise for that mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Colonel, you said that you were approached by Lord Ashdown and your former ambassador over this very question, because Lord Ashdown was unhappy that the dates didn't tie up, et cetera? What -- what do you mean? When were you approached by Lord Ashdown and the former ambassador?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly what I say, sir. I was contacted by Lord Ashdown, who I believe came here to give evidence. I don't know, because I wasn't involved. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: My question -- excuse me, sir. My question is when did he contact you? When?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think -- I think it was prior to Christmas, because there was some intent then for me to come before Christmas. That was cancelled or postponed for various reasons. I then was out of the country for a month. I got back on the 3rd of February and I came here on the 5th, and I presume it was either very early in January this year, 2007, or the back end of 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: When Lord Ashdown -- you didn't call him; he called you, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: When he called you just before Christmas -- now we have the dates right. 2006, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was last Christmas.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Right. Okay. Did -- he initiated the call and give us the substance of the conversation you had with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had apparently written a diary of his trips around Kosovo, and in it from his remembrance of the facts was that he did not see General Ojdanic. He went back to Beograd, and he a meeting with President Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From his recall of events, that statement in paragraph 50, 51, excuse me, was not correct. And that's why I asked Ms. Carter to -- to change that, yesterday, and to inform the Court that an error had been made.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Did he say why he was calling you at the time? Why did he call you, do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because we were we were quite friendly together, and we'd enjoyed one another's company around Kosovo. And I think he was concerned that he wished to give, as I do, under oath a correct version as possible, and as I've said already many times, I apologise for this being incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Did he tell you perhaps at that time that he'd been contacted by the Ojdanic Defence team who had asked him to produce his diaries and any other material he had on the matter and that he had, and that the diaries revealed no such meeting with General Ojdanic, and that there in fact was no such meeting with General Ojdanic to the best of Lord Ashdown's recollection?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't believe he said that to me at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: He didn't tell you about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think so, sir, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Now, if he had not called you, if he had not called you, you would have simply come here and given the evidence that you had previously given in the Milosevic case, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's not correct, sir. As I said, when I arrived here on the 5th and I saw Ms. Carter and the team on the 6th, my first approach to her, and I think she'll bear witness to that, was that I said paragraph 50 and 51 have been muddled up and that needs to be -- if that is the procedure of the Court, and I'm not totally familiar with that obviously in legal terms, that needs to be changed and your -- your side needs to be informed there has been a change.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: But you say you would have come to that conclusion on your own, without discussing it with Lord Ashdown? Would you have come to that conclusion on your own?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I think Lord Ashdown jogged my memory. I -- as I said, I produced over 70 reports. I reported continuously back to the Ministry of Defence. I think the embassy sent something like a thousand telegrams during that very busy year. Mistakes have been made I'm afraid, for which I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Colonel Crosland, that's -- I've made more mistakes than I can tell you about my in my life, so it's not a question -- everyone makes mistakes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I agree, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: But had he not jogged your memory, had he not jogged your memory, is it fair to say, you probably would have come here and given the exact same testimony and evidence you'd previously given in those prior statements; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With respect, sir, I've tried every time I come here to refresh myself and to bring myself back up to date with what has gone on quite some time ago. I was unhappy with it, because I didn't think it was correct. I had made the statement previously. I have apologised for that. I can say no more. I mean -- you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: You didn't discover the mistake prior to testifying in the Milosevic case, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Apparently not, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when you discussed this with Ms. Carter, did you also -- by the way, on the question of, again, Lord Ashdown, I think you -- you still have it wrong, I say respectfully, sir, on Lord Ashdown. In answer to a question, yesterday, by lord -- by the Chief Judge, Judge Bonomy - I said Lord Ashdown and Lord Bonomy - so, Judge Bonomy said, and this is on page 58 yesterday, "Can I be clear about one thing," he said to you,"on the 27th of August, when you observed events at Suva Reka, was Ashdown there?" And you said, "Yes, Your Honour. He was there with the BBC crew and Ambassador Donnelly." Okay. Now, that's not so, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, sir, I think the dates have been muddled up; and whether we got September or August, you know, our asking me to come back to a date ten years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Well, didn't --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: You haven't reviewed your situation reports for when you met with Lord Ashdown? Don't you know that you have a situation report of -- of 28 September 1998, which talks about meeting with Lord Ashdown on 26 and 27th September, 1998? You never met with him in August, and I represent that to you, sir. You never met with him in August?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It may -- there may have been a -- I need to look at the report sir, with -- frankly and honestly, to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. Well the report is K0198390. It's a report of a visit by Judge -- by Lord Ashdown in September 26 and 27 of 1998; and the fact is that, as Lord Ashdown has further noted, he's never been in Kosovo during that period.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, then we've got the wrong date, as simple as that. I took Lord Ashdown twice around Kosovo, and he was there with the BBC, who may well have a film of it, of the shelling of Suva Reka and villages to the West?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And you did indeed take him around in September and December of 1998. We have both of those reports.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you for informing me. I apologise for the date being wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. And by the way, again, in answer to Judge Bonomy's question, you said,"On the 27th of August, when you observed events at Suva Reka, was Ashdown there?" Well, you didn't -- did you observe events at Suva Reka on August 27th? Wasn't that the day of the attache meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is my point, sir. We appear to have muddled up a month -- a date by a month, for which I apologise. I was spent an awful lot of my time in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And when you were discussing these matters with Ms. Carter, did she point out to you at all any inconsistencies, discrepancies in your prior testimony concerning the alleged turnover of this video to General Ojdanic? Was that discussed at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not as far as I'm aware, sir, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I'm going to get to it that a little bit later, but I just want to clear away a few things here on whether or not you gave the video to -- whether you turned over the video to General Ojdanic. And I respectfully submit to you, sir, that I think you're wrong about that, just like you were wrong about Lord Ashdown. And I'll -- we'll go into why I'm saying that. And by the way, sitting here now, sitting here now, before I get into my questions, are you prepared to concede if I make a sufficient demonstration to you, that you got that wrong, too. That, in fact, you never really showed this video to General Ojdanic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I represent, as I've said, the video was given to the Vojska Jugoslavija. Whether General Ojdanic or anyone else looked at it, I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Oh, so you don't even know if he looked at it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With great respect, sir, I'm not going to tell a very senior general to look at a video. If he has not or other people or his staff have not looked at it, that is their business. I'm -- you know, it would be extremely inquisitive and rude of me to demand a general or anyone else to look at evidence that he may not wish to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Then I must have misunderstood your testimony, yesterday, then. You never did see him look at a video?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've just said to you, sir. I don't know whether he has ever looked at it. It was handed over as a demonstration that what was being reported on a daily basis by various members of the Attache Association, mainly by myself and other people, that we had evidence that the Vojska Jugoslavija and MUP were carrying out combined operations that were both damaging and not helping the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia's cause against an insurgent operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So, you didn't show this video to General Ojdanic on August 27th 1998?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I presented it to him or to his staff; and what they did with it, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I presented to him or his staff. There's a difference. There's a difference, sir. Who did you present it to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think at the time Colonel Negovan Jovanovic [Realtime transcript read in error "Negovanovic"], who was the head of FLS, was at this meeting, and I probably gave it to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So you gave the video to Colonel, give me the name again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Colonel Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. You didn't give it to General Ojdanic. You gave it could the Colonel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I passed it had across to the Foreign Liaison Service, which was headed up by Colonel Jovanovic, through which all Attache Association requests for interviews with various personnel, for permission to move across Yugoslavia, all the staffing was done through the Foreign Liaison Service; therefore, that is the entree, a correct entree, for a Defence attache to present any information he wishes to pass.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So sitting here right now, is it fair to say you have no idea whether General Ojdanic ever viewed that video?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've just told you that, sir. I -- it was not my job to ask the General to look at a video, because in my army you would be put in clank.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I had a number of questions, I mean lengthy, to go with prior statements and what -- I'm going to forego that right now. And I don't know, if we ever get into a problem here on time, I would like permission to perhaps come back to that because -- and I'll go on to something else now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What you're suggesting is if there's time at the tend to come back to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, because I have a considerable amount of material on this that I was going to present, quite frankly, to Colonel Crosland, in terms of prior inconsistent statements and that kind -- let me see if can do it in just a few minutes then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But I doubt if it's a productive exercise for you, even what's happened so far might be described as a bit of overkill, Mr. Sepenuk, in view of the role that we play here. It's achieved its objective, though, because you've got to something that you might never have discovered, and you may have reached it by accident. And it's an important piece of evidence that the statement yesterday, even in its revised form, still said, before we excluded it completely. "I showed Ojdanic photographic evidence of the VJ shelling Suva Reka." And that's been the main achievement of what your cross has gained so far. There is one question though. I'd like to ask which may alter you view of this. What was it that actually prompted Mr. Ojdanic to say, "force would be met with appropriate force?"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it was the very precise information that we were passing to General Ojdanic and the VJ staff, that the VJ was actively engaged in operations with the MUP, and they were providing, as I said yesterday, both the direct fire support from tanks, the indirect from artillery, and mortars. And we had had evidence of that, and this was a very controversial issue in -- in both our -- in our eyes and obviously news that General Ojdanic and the staff did not want to hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And was it at the meeting of defence attaches that you gave the video to Ojdanic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, sir, yes. As I've attempted to explain to Your Honour and the Court, the FLS, the Foreign Liaison Section, was the correct staff entry for a defence attache.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that. I just wondering if it was at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic has a comment about the record, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, page 30, line 23, and then line 5 on page 31, Colonel Crosland said the name of the officer that he was liaising with. It should be have been Negovan Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just for the transcript. The transcript reflects a different name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Visnjic. Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Colonel, I'm going to be getting to the briefing a little bit later on, but before that I want to ask you a few questions about the KLA and get some background for the briefing and generally for the benefit of the Trial Chamber. Is it fair to say that at least by early 1998, there was a genuine fear on the part of the Serbian authorities that the then KLA insurgence movement would gain strength and they would lose control over Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is quite correct. And I, with the many conversations I had with both General Perisic and General Dimitrijevic, attempted to explain, having had considerable experience in dealing with counter-insurgency involvements, that this -- this insurgency was not going to be a simple task to achieve and could take a very long time in both men and materiel and had severe political implications down line. So I think my advice and my -- and unfortunately my prognosis and diagnosis was correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And do you agree, Colonel, that taking Kosovo out of Serbia is like taking Wales out of England?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You've taken that from a statement I made.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I certainly have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That got me into a lot of trouble. Perhaps why my career ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: That is correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And you when the KLA took up arms against the sovereign state of Serbia, Serbia clearly had the right to respond to the terrorist tactics of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is -- again, you may obtained that from a statement I made. I don't know. But that is entirely my position, and it remains my position to this -- to this very day, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I am taking it from a statement. I will say this. I am taking it from the same statement that Mr. O'Sullivan uses. A statement you gave just four months prior to the statement that was submitted by the Prosecution, your October 2006 statement. This other statement was made by you, sir, in June of 2006, prior to the Prosecution who is preparing the Haradinaj trial. And all the Trial Chamber has right now is that one statement you made, October 2006, which only contains about a page, a little over a page on the KLA. And, again, to get a complete picture here for the Trial Chamber, I'm going to refer quite extensively to the statements you gave to the Prosecution in preparation for the Haradinaj case. And just so there's no doubt about it, in your opinion the KLA was indeed a terrorist organisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Now, I want to deal with just a few aspects of the KLA and the size, its membership, its weaponry, that kind of thing. And you have it starting out as an insurgent force, which you now agree is, of course, a terrorist operation of some 400 men, which later grew to 3.000 men, or you're not precise, but that's roughly your testimony. And I want to -- I want to go over what you said in your earlier statement, June 30 2006. And in paragraph 42 page 7 of that statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Respectfully, Your Honour, I believe Mr. Sepenuk is misquoting this witness's testimony. He's been very clear all along he believed there was approximately 400 fighters. He said that repeatedly in the trial. I don't recall any testimony where he said they grew to 3.000 men, as noted on page 35, line 8 by Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Actually, it was in yesterday's testimony. If we go to the break, I can't it right now but it was in yesterday's testimony. And I don't think we need be detained by that Your Honour. With Your Honour's permission, I'll go on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Colonel Crosland can tell us, again, what he reckons was the ultimate maximum strength of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think Mr. Sepenuk is possibly correct. The figure of 3.000 did come came up yesterday. Yesterday is a bit of a blur. I have repeatedly said I -- there was a hard-core of approximately 400. This may have may have grown as the possibility of the KLA being successful or however you want to put it, and therefore it may have grown to a considerable number beyond that. But whether 3.000 -- I would -- I personally would stick with 400 and a lot of hangers-on that can see a victory march in Pristina at the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And those hangers-on, I think you opined, yesterday, might have been about 3.000?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With respect to Ms. Carter, I will accept that as, yeah, as hangers-on. Let's not get too, with respect, hung up about people just wearing uniforms for the sake of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. Now, on paragraph, again, paragraph 42 of your statement of June 2006, 3D510, you said,. "The KLA started from a very fledgling organisation and matured after the beating they took in the fall of 1998. They responded well by building up their capacity and made quantum leaps when it came to manpower, weapons, structure, et cetera. The KLA definitely had a political and military wing, and they were complementary. In these sense, they were similar to the IRA. The KLA was organised but to call the body at the top a General Staff might be misnaming it." I'm simply asking you, sir, whether that's a true statement. By the way you did state -- in your statement, you said that everything was true to the best of your knowledge and belief.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. With respect, I made that statement, and I think I made the -- the similarity between the KLA and the IRA because this had come up before. The idea of a General Staff and brigades of KLA throughout the province of Kosovo was, in my humble opinion, something we'd done in various other operations around the world, where we call a brigade, like the Londonderry Brigade is about eight men. A brigade is 3.000. It looks very good on an intelligence map and you might guess, and I am not very keen on some of the intelligence that one is being given during operations that I have taken part in. So I -- I don't say that flippantly. But I say we need to be careful as to the General Staff of the KLA, I think is an overstatement, as I say it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: We'll get to that a little bit later?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And in paragraph 6 of your statement, you said,"The heavy handed response of the Serbian forces definitely played into the hands of the KLA."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: "They gained massive support from the diaspora but also from the international community, the international media, et cetera. This support later translated into massive financial assistance that could be used to buy logistical supplies. I have seen some pretty impressive KLA weapons depot, including in Glodjane, Ramush Haradinaj's headquarters." True statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir. And I believe that was in November or September, November of 1998 when, as I think I've said in many statements, there was a quantum improvement, both in the way they behaved, their uniforms, and the armaments that they had -- they had got through the system.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: But still 400 men, right? You're sticking with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I would stick with 400, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Even though they had some headquarters in some 24 locations and in your October 31 2006 statement, paragraph 26, Prosecution Exhibit 2645, you mentioned 23 or 4 separate locations where the KLA had headquarters. I won't name all the cities, but you know them, of course: Racak and Malisevo, Junik, Sedlare?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're absolutely correct, sir. Twenty-four locations. If there were 15 to 20 in each, then you've got about 400. Now, that's my --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. We'll talk a little bit more about that later, too?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And then in paragraph 7, you state, "Also, there was a massive influx of volunteers, including foreign nationals; Dutch, French, British et cetera. Ten to 15 percent of the KLA were what I would call hard-core, remaining 85, 90 percent joined out of different reasons ranging from sense of responsibility to a desire to be considered a hero in the end; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: You can just say yes or no. You don't have to comment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's entirely correct, sir. And if we look to the march that took place in Kosovo and in Pristina at the end of it, I think that bears out what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. And then in paragraph 27 of the statement, you said, "The KLA -- KLA's core members believed in their cause, and they were prepared to do whatever they saw as necessary to reach their goal. There are no angels. Some of them are thugs. From my experience on the ground, it is leer could me that Ramush and his brother were involved in criminal activities." And now I realise I believe that I'm repeating what Mr. O'Sullivan said, that Ramush is up it to his neck and even to this day. And you did make that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Now I also -- I want to move briefly now to the question of KLA tactics, as reflected in this statement, and I'd like to start at paragraph 9, page 3. You said, "The KLA used classic insurgency tactics straight out of Mao Tse-tung's good book. They first established a strong base in the villages, and then basically tried to hold on until NATO intervened. To say that the KLA only had political goals, independence, et cetera, is very naive. They also carried out a policy that was translated on the ground by the military wing of the KLA." You said that, correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, and that has come to fruition.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. And paragraph 43, you state, page 7, 3D510, "In my previous statements, I have talked about a big change in the KLA's level of organisation capacity, which happened in October 1998. I think the international community has to answer questions for that sudden change because it was radical. The KLA filled in the void when the Serbs withdrew in compliance with international agreements. The OSCE's Verification Mission gave them an umbrella under which to operate." Can you explain what you meant by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I had serious doubts all the way along when the ACTORD from NATO was being signed, and that the three combat groups of the Vojska Jugoslavija correctly and with military precision withdrew back into barracks. I warned the various authorities that if we did not fill the vacuum, then the KLA would fill it. And, in fact, as these three battle groups were moving back to barracks, to Prizren, Pristina, and Urosevac, three MUP were killed just west of Pristina on the road. Now, to the credit of the Serbian security forces, they kept their fingers off the trigger and maintained their discipline.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now, I -- sorry. With respect sir, part of the my reporting, as an extremely experienced and senior officer, is to try and give both political and military knowledge to my seniors, because obviously at this stage there was planning going on for whatever future events may or may not take place. Therefore, one was trying to give, if you will, a broad brush or an overview of the entire situation, because there were very little -- there were very few other people apart from myself actually on the ground at this particular time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. And then finally on this will question of tactics, you say on paragraph 46 of this statement 3D510,"I think that part of the reason why the KLA moved in quickly is the result of a 'jungle drums' factor." Jungle drums in quotes. "In Kosovo, the word spreads real really quickly. Villages are really closely knit. The KLA probably had a good communication system in a technical sense, too. But I think word of mouth contributed to the speediness with which the KLA moved in." Correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. And I make that statement because very early on in 1996, when I first went down to Kosovo, I was struck by the huge Albanian population; and when I made this statement coming back to Belgrade, it concerned people that the factors of the population were not correct. I mean, people said at the time that the Serbs were still in the -- in the majority and the Albanians in the minority. And from my view of the situation and carrying out, I will readily admit, not a technical census but a fairly good census of going around, most of the villages and speaking to the Albanians, you would go to a house or a village of 20 houses from which you may expect, I don't know, a hundred people you would get 4 or 500 people. And when you multiplied all the villages up, there was some very rough and simple mathematics, which I will accept, but I came out with a figure of nearly 2 million Albanians and about, as I said before, about 400.000 Serbs. So it was very clear to me from a very early age or very early in the time I was there, that the Serbs may have been technically in control of the government and other organisations. But the real powerhouse was with the Albanians, and that was factor that I thought my seniors should know about.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So a massive Albanian population, being fair to say also, a fairly large number of which may very well have elected to support the KLA in their activities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think sadly the initial percent, as I said yesterday, most Kosovo Albanians there really didn't want either the VJ, the MUP, or the KLA. I'm afraid the -- the very robust actions of the VJ and the MUP did damage in the long-run, many of the Albanians who eventually did turn towards supporting the KLA. Now, that -- I would emphasise that there was an element of fear in that by people like Ramush and that continues today as you're -- you're very well aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Now, I want to -- on that, I wanted to ask you for your comments on a Prosecution exhibit. It's Exhibit 2136, and what is it is a report of 22 June 1998 by ECMM. And would you tell the Chamber what that stands for. European Community Monitoring Mission; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It's a blank memory there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I want to read from part of that exhibit that talks about UCK membership, and remember this is 22 June. And here what it says, Colonel: "Throughout" -- would it help you if I put it up, for you to look at?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've got it. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. And could you scroll up to UCK membership, please. Yes, okay. Little bit higher. Okay. Up -- no. Up. Thank you. Here's what the ECMM group says: "Throughout the pass week, the team has encountered probably more UCK at check-points than Serb and has been greeted by all sorts of individuals from local villagers carrying shotguns to masked UCK declaring themselves as leaders. The gradation of UCK member that we had previously suspected seems correct, with numerous villagers carrying weapons and even boys helping with the construction of trenches. But uniformed membership seems more substantial than first envisaged and is probably the result of more resent recruiting following the expansion of UCK-held territory. The hard-core UCK membership appear almost invariably to have emerged from the diaspora with, a significant number from Germany in particular, Austria, and Switzerland. They are confident and driven and occasionally nervous but nearly always courteous. It seems they are not aware of ECMM and so far have not wished to take advantage of our presence to communicate their wishes. Indeed, the overall impression is that they care little for the international community whom they distrust; and whilst NATO airstrikes might be convenient for them, they have -- they have no intention of waiting for them. The larger family unit, to which an Albanian so often derives support, is still the most plausible overall structure on to which the UCK is attached and will remain their greatest strength. In this way, membership of the UCK becomes unlimited." "In this way, membership in the UCK becomes unlimited." I've repeated it, Colonel. What do you think? Some truth to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With respect, sir, I think I've actually endorsed what you said in this particular report. I mean, in my reports, I said in middle 1998, in technical terms, there were four main routes across Kosovo. Three of those were actually blocked at Rudnik, Lapusnik, and Stimlje, leaving the VJ a mountainous route to get across to Prizren and the western areas. I visited all these three positions. They were manned by 15 to 20 fighters. Compared to what the Vojska Jugoslavija and the MUP had, these positions, I walked through these positions. I saw the trenches. These were shell scrapes. Now, having -- I don't know. I think you have some military service, sir. Certainly, I wouldn't want to be in one of these shell scrapes if shell-fire came down. These were immature and insignificant defensive positions. I made a comment to I think General Velickovic at one stage on a defence attache evening, that I just didn't understand why the Vojska Jugoslavija and the MUP were allowing or technically allowing the UCK to control "about 50 percent of Kosovo." Now, what this statement here says from the ECCM [sic], and forgive me I can't remember the date of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: June, June 22nd?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And the points they make about the exit tended family, I think I've just explained that there was a massive, in relative terms, imbalance between the population; the Kosovo Albanian population and the Serbian population. And many of these had come from -- from Albania, which was in a state of chaos from the 1977 disturbances.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So I would not disagree with that. It's entirely in line with what I've told you on the bigger picture of the KLA and the potential for major numbers to appear. What I go back to is the people who are actually prepared to go out and face a considerable force by the VJ and the MUP, and I would -- I would maintain that the hard-core fighters were still in the region of 400.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay all right fine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But I accept, and I think I've given you evidence, that there was huge potential to draw on, should it become clear that the KLA were going to be successful, how you would like to put the phrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. You've given us your position now on various aspects of the KLA. I'd like now to turn to what the VJ position was. And I'm going to do that by referring to a document dated 28 July 1998. And it's 4D137, and it's a directive signed by General Perisic. It's to the command of the 1st 2nd 3rd Army and other groups to deploy the Yugoslav Army for securing the state border with Albania. Units and facilities in the area of Kosovo and Metohija and crush the armed rebel forces. Again, July 28, 1998, 4D137. Now, in the first paragraph, it states, and again this is an order signed by General Perisic, "The Albanian terrorists in Kosovo and Metohija have at their disposal about 15.000 armed personnel, about 5.000 personnel for various forms of logistical support, and approximately another 2.500 trained terrorists in the Republic of Albania. In a very short time, the number of terrorists may be increased by another 15.000 people." I will pause. Again, this is signed by General Perisic. You had many meetings, did you not, with General Perisic and his counter intelligence advisor, General Dimitrijevic; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. And I don't believe these figures were ever presented to me. If they were, I don't recall them. I can only restate that when I was on the ground for most of this time that the figures like this were not borne out by what I saw. And the -- the actions of the KLA then, because for the majority they were, as I've said already many were on the back foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I simply wanted to put before you what the VJ saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If that's what their Chief of Staff says, then fine.
