utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. Now you also, again, had a number of meetings with General Dimitrijevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And a very good relationship with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Considered him a fairly good intelligence officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think he'd been a long time in the position.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Right. And he had very good intelligence on the KLA, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's what I've said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Right. And some of the intelligence was in the form of interception of KLA communications?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The -- the Vojska Jugoslavija and the MUP were extremely good on the counter -- on the electronic intelligence, in the end, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Well, General Dimitrijevic, on 21 January, 1999, in the 9th session of the collegium of the General Staff of the Yugoslav army,- Prosecution Exhibit 939, said, on pages 17 and 18 of that document, he said -- he had a map there, and he said,"These blue areas are sectors controlled by the so-called KLA. As you can see from this diagram, the approximate number of people armed and organised into units is between 12 and 15.000." That was the assessment of General Dimitrijevic, who you agree is a pretty good intelligence officer with pretty good contacts in determining KLA membership. Okay, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I accept what you're saying. That the fact is on the ground, we did not see 12 to 15.000. I -- throughout my life, I'm interested in reporting facts as accurately, and with the experience that I've had not in blowing up the picture for whichever side wishes to blow up that particular picture. Now, what General Dimitrijevic says, fine. I've never seen this document before, I don't believe. I'm seen a hell of a lot of documents, and I'm not certain I've seen this one. But if he made that statement, then I accept it. But I'm saying what I personally saw in the time that I toured throughout the area was -- was, again, about 400 hard-core terrorists. The fact that you could add onto that through the extended family very, very quickly up into the thousands, as happened when Pristina was freed, then I think bears out what I am saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. Now, General, I want to -- Colonel --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's a very quick promotion, sir, but I'll accept it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: The open thing higher is lord?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We'll wait for that for next new year's honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: The 3D511 is next exhibit I'd like to discuss with you. I will say as a slight aside, Colonel, and this is very little levity in the trial. All the members of the Defence team refer to each other as general, so I'm into that habit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've obviously joined the wrong army, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Now, 3D511 is a meeting of 25 June 1998 with you, if that could be put up. And it's a record of a meeting that you had with General Jovanovic? Is that the same general you spoke about before, the general you allegedly handed the video to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He's not a general, but a colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Not a general, but a colonel. If I said general, I am blaming my colleagues, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wish they had made him a general. He was a very good friend.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: A very good friend, and I take it a good and honest man of integrity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He, actually, was one of the last couple of Vojska Jugoslavija officers to be trained in our Staff College.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So the summary he gave your meeting is more likely than not to be accurate; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Apart from my name being spelt wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I'll just start, and we'll read it together as we go along.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And it says here, "The main views given at the meeting," and he says, "The so-called KLA," this is his meeting with you on June 25, 1998, "is increasingly revealing its fundamental characteristic of a terrorist organisation which has no qualms in liquidating its members for the slightest disobedience. Something that has become more apparent recently."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry. I would accept that entirely that there was a vicious -- as I've made clear in statements, the discipline was harshly enforced at times, and people who were not pro the organisation were at considerable risk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: All right. And if you don't mind a detour, Colonel, and you can stop looking at that exhibit, I do want to go back. I'm sorry to say omitted a few questions on the prior exhibit, which was, again, 4D137. We'll get back to 3D511 very shortly, but if the usher could put back up 4D137. Now, we discuss numbers and General Dimitrijevic's figure of 15 -- of some 13, 15.000, whatever it was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: In the second paragraph there, it says, "By carrying out terrorist activities in Kosovo and Metohija, the terrorists have succeeded in taking control of about 30 percent of the territory; the general area of Drenica, Malisevo, Studencani, Blace, and the area of Jasik, Junik, Smonica, as well as Pristina, Glodjane, and Jablanica." Correct? "And spread their influence to about 40 percent of the territory."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's exactly in line with what I forecast, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. In fact in your statement of 30 June 2006, in paragraph 23, you said,"During the same period in the summer of 1998, the KLA technically controlled about 70 percent of Kosovo. I say technically because they could stage insurgency attacks on the Serbs on this territory." You go on to say,"Of course, the situation was very fluid and the percentage changed over time. I explained this more fully in the daily reports that I wrote, which are attached to my Professor statements." Fair enough?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And in the third paragraph, the general, says this, the order says this, the directive, "In order to accomplish their goals," in fact, why you don't you read it, sir. You read it, since you're much better at pronouncing these names than I am?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sepenuk, I hope you are bearing the time in mind, because you're expanding this cross examination to quite an extent by a fair bit of repetition and also by reading things, where you could pose focused questions rather than putting up documents and reading them out and asking the witness whether he agrees. The questions could be much more focused for our purposes. Of course, if you're going to be able to do it within the time that you expect to have, fine. But I suspect you may have difficulty.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I'll shorten it, Your Honour. Let me just let me just skip to the paragraph 2 -- page 2, about the Yugoslav Army's deployment so far. And it says, "The Yugoslav Army has undertaken specific measures against terrorism," and I'm going to be very brief here now. And I will quote now, directly, the following language, "Through its presence and by carrying out the training in the entire territory of Kosovo and Metohija, the army has had a repelling effect with regard to the Siptar Albanian terrorist forces, and it has offered direct assistance to the forces of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia." Is that correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's what's written there, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. And did you have discussion was General Perisic about this, about the KLA, and about the MUP and VJ working together?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I -- yes. We did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And General Dimitrijevic, also?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. And this is in line with that, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is what is what is written here, and I would agree with the majority of it. What exactly happens on the ground, as I've said before sometimes, it sometimes doesn't bear out what happens here. But we'll see what is brought before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: All right. Let's go back now to 3D511. That's your meeting with Colonel Jovanovic. And in page 2 of that meeting, summarised by the colonel, he says this: "The situation" -- he said, that you said, "The situation is also rendered more complex by the fact that in Kosovo Metohija, there is no front line separating the two opposed forces, but instead that there are terrorist groups which set up base mostly in settled place with an ethnically pure population supportive of the idea of Kosovo, a republic." And by that, very briefly, Colonel, you meant what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly what I what has been written here, and I think I made the statement to the Court this morning. I was extremely concerned that the -- the total imbalance of the population of Kosovo, Albanian to Serb, with this insurgency movement was not going to be an easily problem to solve. I think I've state that had that on several occasions. And with this meeting having gone back to the United Kingdom, I made it clear to various people I briefed - and they are all in the front paragraph there, some very senior people - that we had an extremely difficult problem which was not going to be solved easily.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So you were extremely concerned, and needless to say, the VJ was also extremely concerned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Understandably, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes. And then finally on this document, number 4 on page 2, paragraph 4, and it says, "The main reason why the MZ international community failed to characterize the KLA as a terrorist organisation is the impact that the mass media and reporting from Kosovo Metohija have, which is still in favour of the Albanians, in connection with this he," meaning you, Colonel Crosland, "suggested that the officials of the government of Serbia be more aggressive in their interviews and an in official comments on events when talking to international reporters and TV channels." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. And I also would ask you to look at the at the -- four paragraph four -- the third paragraph: "This is not the first time that Colonel Crosland has tried to convince us that he's been doing his utmost to have an objective view of the Kosovo situation adopted in Great Britain and broader by the multi-international organisations. He insisted these view were also shared by Ambassador Donnelly." So I think that's entirely in line with the overall picture that I've been trying to paint of a fair and firm assessment of what is going on throughout this period in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Including that Serbian officials should be a little bit more aggressive in presenting their case; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely. Because we had up until then, I think very little-- I think we had one or maybe two briefings to show or to put together the Vojska Jugoslavija - we were accredit to them only - their view. I did say that I thought there was mileage in making this a message to the Attache Association which included all the attaches. With respect, sir, I must remind you that only some of the NATO attaches, about six countries, were actually touring and, therefore, had the intimate knowledge that I had. So the question of trying to inform the international community and the Albanians were without doubt very much better at informing the diaspora to support them in this project.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And on August 27 1998, which was now the briefing by General Ojdanic of the defence attaches, didn't he adopt some of the points you were making? He talked about a double standard. He talked about the -- blaming the international community blaming the VJ, when in fact much of the blame rested on the KLA, that kind of thing. He said that, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, when you go back to the report, I said I was fairly condemning about the report. I think I said it was a wooden briefing, and also that his remark at the end of it, "force would be met with force," which I took rightly or wrongly - and I can stand corrected on that - that the same very harsh -- harsh military manoeuvres - I would call them crude with respect - which were being displayed on the international media, were you not doing the Serbian cause any good. And that is the point, with respect, sir, which I think has to be made; that the media now is incredibly invasive and intensive on military operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Colonel, please, just answer -- please, just listen to my question. He did say that the international community was applying a double standard, that it was not condemning terrorism by the KLA but was focusing on acts of the Serbs. Didn't he say that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe he did, and I've actually agreed with you on that case. And I made the point when I made the point to my own Ministry of Defence that the -- the Serbian viewpoint was way behind in intensity of that being produced by the Kosovo Albanian and the diaspora at large, which was supporting them massively in both finance and manpower.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. And he said forth -- we don't go into this. Again, I think there was ample detail on it, yesterday. He set forth the duties of the VJ, four duties. And you agree with all of them, don't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They make military sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: They make military sense?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was nice to hear that he was now accepting what we've been telling him, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: You don't think he would have come to that conclusion -- in other words, you told him that what you got to do is protect VJ installations and protect --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With respect, there was -- without being rude to the Court, I think we're slightly splitting hairs here. As a military man, one respects that General Ojdanic, as a professional soldier, was carrying out his duties per se. It was nice to hear him send -- admit that the VJ's main tasks had now changed, quite understandably, in the view that the situation had deteriorated as we were going along. So I have no problem with that at all, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And the MUP needed help, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I think I stated that. From General Dimitrijevic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: All right. And he -- at the conference, he said that the MUP and the VJ were cooperating, primarily to protect lines of communication. You have no trouble with that, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't have any trouble with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the way it was being carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: All right. And you pointed out -- now we no know you didn't show him the video, but apparently you say you orally pointed out to him about observing direct indirect fire, which was creating not a good situation, and the General agreed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He got this from me then, and then he, I would presume, when I met with General Perisic and General Dimitrijevic, they would have passed on the concerns, without blowing my own trumpet, of probably one of the most experienced DAs there. So I think my views were listened to, as someone who is attempting to give both a fair and firm report on what was going on in an increasingly complex and difficult situation, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: That's all I have, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sepenuk. Good timing. We need to break now, Mr. Crosland, for half an hour or so. We'll go into closed session while you leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Crosland.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm Djuro Cepic, one of the lawyers for General Lazarevic, and I'm going to have a few questions for you. Mr. Crosland, in the statement that you provided in June 2006, in paragraph 8, you pointed out that the KLA, in the course of 1998, pursued a policy of ethnic cleansing. Further on, you say that there is no doubt the entire region west of Decani has been cleaned by the KLA from all the non-Albanians. When you mentioned that region, did you also imply Junik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. I'm trying to recall that certainly the area, the mountain area along the frontier between Albania and Kosovo at that particular time, the villages I saw had been destroyed. Junik, I think, was still in the hands of Kosovo Albanians, I believe, KLA. I don't know whether that answers your question entirely or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I believe so. Thank you. And it was about the ethnic cleansing by the KLA, and you adhere by what you said in your statement that you provided in June 2006.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, and I think the -- the villages there in that area, in the very mountainous areas, led directly to well-worn paths which went back to Albania, from where the KLA was receiving its resupply.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Can we then say that the axis across Junik was actually one of the most strategic points for the KLA when it came to the supply with weapons and replenishing their ranks with men? Wouldn't that be correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are correct, sir. That was one the main areas, as well as Pastrik as well to the south by Djakovica. I'm sorry, not Djakovica, but Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Crosland. Paragraph 12 of your statement, dating October 2006, you say that a majority of the villages in the region especially Junik was razed in spring of 1998. What part of spring? What time of spring was it when Junik was razed? Was it maybe the May, the month of May of that year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Without referring directly back to what -- to what I said, sir, I'm not entirely certain. But there was an ongoing battle raging across the Junik, Ponosevac, Prilep, Rznic area for about three months, and there was extremely intense activity by both sides. Because, as you said, there was an area of strategic importance to the KLA and was one of Ramush Haradinaj's key areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That was a reference, I think, to paragraph 41 of the statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Now, Your Honour, if you allow me, paragraph 12, last sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. By spring, it was April, May, June, July. The battleground, if I may call it that, raged for about three to four months over this area because of its key issue to both sides. It was an area which the MUP and the VJ required to hold. And they had, if you will, a quasi-front line which went down the road from Pec through Decani down to Djakovica, which was an attempt to keep a, what I would call, a thin red line, and then to try and exclude the border area from incursion mainly from Albania. So I would accept your statement, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: During the period that you've just mentioned and further on, Junik itself was held by the strong KLA forces, wouldn't that be right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think, I'm correct, in thinking, sir, that it was held. And at one stage when we went into -- on several occasions, when we visited there, it may have been retaken by your own forces. But if we're asking specific details, then I need to look back at specific reports, sir. But I think the situation was fairly fluid in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Crosland, during the period between the 20th and 25th of June, 1998, Mr. Holbrooke visited Junik. His visit was covered by many international agencies. And in those footages, you can see a single destroyed house, which means that the village was completely intact at the time. Am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I recall the picture. I also recall him sitting with a KLA soldier, which caused intense anger within Yugoslavia. Whether there was one house which was standing, I don't recall that particular picture. But when I visited the place, there was -- there was considerable damage, and that was throughout this period of flux and fighting in this particular area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think Mr. Cepic's point is -- has been lost in translation. Your point was that there was no house damage, is that it, or are you saying there was one house dammed?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not a single one was damaged, as far as you could see in those footages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is a very specific point. He's saying that in late June 1998, that village was intact.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that may well have been correct. It certainly wasn't intact when I saw it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, can you help us with when you saw it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well I -- well, I stated, in paragraph 12, most villages in this region particularly Junik were razed in spring 1998. The point I'm trying to make, Your Honour, is that during this period, there was a flux of fighting which occurred in and around Junik, which was a key point. And during this period of the spring, Junik was systematically destroyed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The point is being put to you is that in June, which I think we can call the summer, Junik was intact.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I would disagree with that, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now Mr. Cepic is going to show us the film.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [In English] Unfortunately, I haven't got that film with me, but probably we will show to this Honourable Trial Chamber during the Defence case. And also I can show something -- something from our collection of potential evidence of exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the Registrar now prepare 5D99,.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And during -- while this is being done, Mr. Crosland, do you know that on the 15th of August, 1998, the KLA forces were neutralised in Junik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, sir, I would -- I would not accept "neutralised," as such. I did -- I think they did suffer a reverse. But in my in my opinion, and for what it is worth, throughout Kosovo we had a very flexible situation for most of the time, where there would be Serbian security force advance and clearance of various areas, and then they would move out and the KLA would regroup. Now, if we start picking individual dates, as I said, it was a very flexible situation, which I think I've indicated in several reports, and we've spoken about during this hearing anyway. So I don't question your date, sir, at all. All I'm saying is that in my opinion, it was a flexible, manoeuvrable feast, if you will, where sometimes the KLA was in the ascendance and other times the Serbian security forces were in evidence. And I can't say any more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Crosland, I have a lot of questions. That is why I'm going to put them in a very clear and concise way, and I would also like to ask you for your cooperation and for as short answers as possible. On the 16th of August, the village of Junik was visited by a number of foreign diplomats in order to see what the situation was really like, and they didn't find Junik to be razed or destroyed. Are you familiar with that? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, there was a picture with Mr. Holbrooke in which there was a member of the KLA, which upset, severely upset --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That was June, Mr. Crosland. We have to move ahead. We're talking about 16th of August, and the point is being made that there was an international visit then and, again, the village was not destroyed. Now, what I think we're trying to get to is the point at which you have seen this village destroyed, but it doesn't seem that you're able to remember that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not able to remember it, sir, without referring to specific reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Were you not invited by the Prosecution in preparation for your evidence here to do that exercise; go over the reports, and look at your statement in the light of -- or compile a statement in the light of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I was. But as you're I'm sure aware, sir, with respect, there have been many statements that are being made, and we may not have covered this particular area. For which, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Except for paragraph 12 says, very clearly, "particularly, Junik was razed in the spring of 1998." That looks like a specific piece of information that you were conveying.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, sir, I stand by what I say. If that is against what Mr. Cepic is staying, then we have a disagreement, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: On the screen, you have one of the reports by the army of Yugoslavia, to be more precise by the 3rd Army. And if you look at the last paragraph of that report, the commander of the army, which at the time was General Samardzic, stated that Junik had not been destroyed, that it wasn't razed, that there were no civilian victims, that there were no mass graves for which the world was accusing the Serbian side. These are the facts that nobody ever disputed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, I don't dispute what is said here. I didn't give this -- this briefing. I cannot be responsible for what the mass media produces. I made my specific reports at the time that I saw Junik under heavy fire. The place was razed. Now, that was in the spring of 1998. I'm sorry, I can't be more specific than that. That's all I can really offer on this particular subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Crosland, I believe that you know Colonel Ciaglinski, a member of the Kosovo Verification Commission and a colonel of the UK army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know him, yes, sir, Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Did you communicate with him during his tour of duty in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe he was the military -- military aide to General DZ, or Drewienkiewicz, as we said. I think I was responsible for the briefing of the Kosovo Verification Mission when they arrived in Belgrade and for introducing them down into Kosovo; and then obviously under Ambassador Walker and General DZ, as we call him, they deployed their forces into Kosovo. But I would -- I would not say that we had frequent contact between us, as far as I'm able to recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: That meeting when you met them took place on Saturday, the 17th October, 1998, at the British embassy in Belgrade. Wouldn't that be correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, if you say so, that is correct. I don't -- I don't specifically recall that. But, as I've said to you already, we -- we carried out a briefing prior to their deployment, and I then went with them on their deployment into the area and then left them to -- to sort their own modus operandi out.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Crosland, Colonel Ciaglinski testified in this courtroom in this same case and confirmed that on the 24th of January, 1999, he had visited Junik, that he had spoken to the villagers there, and that the villagers had not pointed out anything of importance to him. Can we believe his words and to what he saw and noticed at the time when he was there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, as I can say, I have stated here, and as far as my memory is correct, that there was -- there was considerable damage in the area of Junik.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Do you know that in the summer of 1998, in the month of July, a team of the High Commissioner For Refugees visited the area, visited Djakovica and spoke to the representatives of the army, and that they expressed their gratitude with regards to the army's behaviour? Are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with that exact statement, no, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the High Commissioner For Refugees of the United Nations, Mrs. Sadako Ogata, visited Kosmet in December, that she visited Prizren, Pec, and Decani? That was in 1998, in December 1998. Are you familiar with that fact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not -- I'm not familiar with the fact she visited, and there were many, many organisations visiting all the time, some of which we communicated with and many which we did not. But at this particular stage, if your point is --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe that you know Mr. Shaun Byrnes, who was the representative of the American KDOM?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I do, sir, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Do you know that on the 21st of October, 1998, he visited the command of the Pristina Corps in Pristina, and that he expressed his satisfaction with the behaviour of the army of Yugoslavia, to be more precise, of the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the answer to that must be yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With respect, sir, I'm being forced into a position here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please answer that question for me, yes or no, because I'm going to deal with this issue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know whether that happened or not, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the answer is no, you don't know. Now, Mr. Cepic, we've had this situation before. This is what I describe as Milosevic-style cross-examination. You are making propositions that you know perfectly well the witness is not going to be able to say anything about. And if you think it is necessary to do that because it's somehow or remember presenting your case - and I know there's a rule about that - then please don't feel obliged to do so. It's a quite unnecessary way of cross-examining a witness. You should deal with things that you know he will be able to comment on properly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. With your leave, I would like to offer a sentence for basis of this question was fact that Mr. Shaun Byrnes and Mr. Crosland were the representatives of their respective KDOMs. And I believe they communicated closely during their tour of duty in Kosovo. That was the basis of examination even in the Milosevic trial. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, Mr. Crosland, you mentioned the shelling of Malisevo, and you said that it had happened in mid-July. You did not cross paths with the Serb forces. You left Malisevo and you left them on the road to Malisevo. Were you on your way back from the KLA headquarters at the time when this happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went into Malisevo on two occasions, if I remember correctly. One where I was taken by the KLA into Malisevo, and as I said in my evidence, I was there for two hours detained by the KLA, who didn't accept the licna karta that I held under allegiance to the Vojska Jugoslavija. On the second occasion, I went back into Malisevo, and I met this joint Vojska Jugoslavija and met this MUP force as stated. As I stated, I then went back a third time with the G8 ambassadors, and Malisevo, the area of the marketplace, and most of the housing had been completely destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Crosland, I asked you a very specific question, and I would kindly ask for a specific answer. You said, yesterday, that in mid-July, Malisevo had come under the attack of the Serb forces and that you saw the forces on the way back from Malisevo. My specific question was whether, at that moment, you were on your way back from the KLA headquarters. In other words, had you been there before that? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said to you already, sir, I've been to Malisevo. I was interrogated in the KLA headquarters there, which was to the left-hand side of the road, close to where the MUP station was eventually produced, in a house that is decorated with animals and all sorts of things. And I then came back up the road and found a Serbian force about or very shortly about to assault the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And you did not stop. You didn't stay on. You just kept on moving.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think, sir, I said on --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- [Previous translation continues] ... that I met. It's written out there for your information, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: So you actually did not witness the operation itself, did you? You didn't see it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Of course, I did not see the operation because --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- we were asked to leave the area. I then took the G8 ambassadors back into Malisevo which, as I said, had been very heavily damaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Now, you've said that you were kept in Malisevo. You were kept there at least twice. At least twice, you were held prisoner by the KLA. You were kept there for a certain period of time. You were detained.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: On one occasion, you were interrogated by a member of the KLA who, according to you, hailed from Middle East, and he was very rough with you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the other occasion, you were detained, together with a French diplomat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on to another topic. Since we've started talking about shelling, yesterday, you told us that you had witnessed the four-hour shelling. What places did you see being shelled? You claim that you saw Junik, Glodjane, Prilep, Ponosevac, all of these being shelled. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, sir. We were on the west-hand side of the road leading from Djakovica north to Decani within certainly sight of Junik, and the multi-rocket launcher battalion was firing from lake Radonjicko. That was coming directly over our head. That conversation went from direct satellite phone back to our foreign secretary who was in the government as Richard's -- Foreign Secretary Cook at the time. That was obviously not a written report. It was an immediate verbal report about the intensity of what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: At the moment when you were watching the shelling of Junik did you also see the other places being shelled, Ponosevac, Suva Reka, Glodjane?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These areas were worked over, to put it in military terms, from time to time. And on this occasion I believe that they -- they were also included in this area. It was -- it was a very -- if I may say so, it was an extremely dangerous area and, as I've said already, it was an area freaked by the KLA and one can understand the concern the Serbian forces. What I've said all way along is that the severity of what was -- what was fired is that -- is that -- what is at issue from my point of view. That's a personal position.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Crosland. You have just confirmed that you yourself saw the shelling of Junik, Glodjane, Ponosevac, Suva Reka, Prilep from the point where you were standing for four hours. Can I please show you a map so that you can indicate the point where you were standing from which you could see all these locations. Can we please see the Exhibit 3D388, and can this please be shown to the witness. On page 67, line 12, in addition to Junik, Glodjane, Ponosevac, I also mentioned Suva Reka, but I am afraid that this last name has been omitted from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's correct further down, I think. It's referred to in line 23.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Suva Reka cannot be seen from that position. That is a mistake that has crept in. Suva Reka is way, way to the east on the road back to Pristina through Prizren, some 30 to 40 kilometres direct line of site.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Maybe even 70, I'd say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe more.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: In other words, from the point where you were standing you could not see the shelling. You could only hear the sound of the shells being fired probably, or maybe you saw something but not the actual shelling.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure where Suva Reka has come from. It may be in The Hague a joint report. When I was reporting on the four-hour shelling from the multi-rocket launcher battalion based on the southern shores of the lake Radonjicko, you could see the strike of -- of shell-fire going into the area of Junik and into Prilep and the Glodjane area. Now, having been under shell-fire myself, you don't have to say can I see the shells landing? Well, probably not. But the damage that I saw in that area was commensurate with heavy shell-fire. The Suva Reka incident I believe was part of the discussion we had this morning when Lord Ashdown was with us and Ambassador Donnelly. The Suva Reka firing came from the area of Blace which is -- which is an artillery position in the middle of the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Let's just deal with this right now. It's not that you saw this. You just came to this conclusion on the basis of what you were hearing, the sounds that you heard, what it was that was being shelled; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is -- that is not correct, sir. As I said, I have been under shell-fire, and the shell -- the multi-rocket launcher battalion were firing more or less directly over our head into the area of Junik and then towards Prilep as well. These are 122-millimetre rockets. They make one hell of a noise, and they land with considerable power.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: But you were not at that artillery position. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With respect, sir, of course I wasn't at that position. We found where that position was.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Paragraph 14 of your statement from October 2006, you say that members of all units, the VJ, the JSO, PJP, and SAJ involved in Kosovo wore bandannas around their heads and other types of non-standard kit to varying degrees. My question: Can you tell us whether you ever saw members of the army of Yugoslavia with bandannas around their heads?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During the period I was down there, there were several means of identification that were being used by the Serbian security forces, and that amounted to --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could you please just be specific, Mr. Crosland. I put a specific question. Did you ever see members of the army of Yugoslavia wearing bandannas around their heads? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the period of time that I was in -- in Kosovo the answer is yes. Specifically, I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: So you cannot give the time or place or position where you saw them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've just answered your question, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Crosland. My learned friend Mr. Sepenuk, General Sepenuk, asked you about tactics of the KLA, and I would like to add something about the tactics of the army of Yugoslavia. You probably know that the tactics of the army of Yugoslavia is defined by the rules of combat; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand that to be correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the rules of combat of the army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe this is a very leading question. What -- what happened in -- in Kosovo as I've already stated many times was a disproportionate use of force against an insurgent operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Crosland, I don't think you need to be quite so defensive about something like this. The rules of combat presumably exist in a documentary form, and the question is: Were you familiar with that document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was never shown this documentary form to the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So there you are. The answer's no. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the army of Yugoslavia extended support only during the neutralisation of strong KLA strongholds? And we heard about that in this courtroom. We heard a number of testimonies to that effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Cepic, that is not an appropriate formulation for a question. If you want to be specific and put some particular testimony that has a direct bearing on what the witness can tell us, then that's fine, but you know that his evidence throughout its two days so far has been to the effect that the support was not confined to the neutralisation of strong KLA strongholds. Now, if you want to challenge that in some specific way, then please do so, but that general proposition you've made is plainly inconsistent with the evidence he's been giving.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave just one sentence. Protected witnesses in this courtroom, K79, K25, did testify to that effect, that the army had not been used in most of the actions that they were carrying out. That was only part of the material corroborating what I have been saying, and that is exactly what I asked Mr. Crosland about just now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you know that that's not been his evidence, and you've asked him a very general question that is quite simply inconsistent with his evidence. But if you want to put any particular point about the way in which the army was used based on the other evidence, then you may do that. But these witnesses, none of them was an expert. None of them was in every part of Kosovo. None of them followed in the wake of Mr. Crosland to make sure they're speaking about the same events. So that approach to the cross-examination is not going to clarify anything in the witness's evidence or undermine it in any way. So let's please ask him questions of what he has direct knowledge of.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 17 of your statement you say that it was your impression that when you providing heavy fire support the VJ or MUP would use radio communications to warn the KLA that an attack was imminent, thereby allowing the population of the village to leave. So that is paragraph 17 of your statement. My question: According to international standards is this not regular procedure to caution the civilian population of possible combat action that is to take place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think with respect, Your Honour, we're muddling up two things here. The first point is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If I can explain it. I thought that paragraph was a comment that was favourable to -- to the VJ and the MUP. What you then say about the extent of damage is another matter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's exactly my point, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You weren't criticising them for warning the population that they might be in the firing-line.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: In accordance with the instructions of the Honourable Presiding Judge, I'm going to ask you about a specific situation. As I already said, Colonel Ciaglinski testified in this courtroom, and he mentioned an army action along the Pristina-Nis road near the village Lebane on the 15th of March, 1999. Previously four colonels had been wounded along the same road, and the army, in order to neutralise the attackers, launched an action of searching those villages. Mr. Ciaglinski's assessment was that it was carried out professionally and according to high standards. Do you agree that Colonel Ciaglinski is competent to make an assessment regarding professional behaviour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please don't answer that, because what this leads to is going round the witnesses asking them whether other witnesses are competent to deal with things. It's for us to judge the competence or otherwise of Colonel Ciaglinski. This witness has made it clear that his knowledge of him is limited, and we probably know more than he does about the things you really need to know about to make a judgement. The only way in which this could begin to be relevant would be if this witness was present on the same occasion. Were you at this event?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not as far as I know, Your Honour, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So please move on to something else, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The reason was the fact that Colonel Ciaglinski said that on that occasion the army was using tanks. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Crosland, in your statement you said that different cannons were used of 20, 30, and 40-millimetre calibres respectively for direct engagement on the ground in contravention of the Geneva Conventions, and you state that in paragraphs 18 and 53 of your statement. Could you please tell me where it was that you saw a 40-millimetre cannon in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, with -- with respect, I saw and collected a number of calibres of empty cases ranging from 122 -- 120-millimetre tank shells just outside Malisevo to 30, 40, 20-millimetre, 12.5, 5.5, 7.62, short, long, you name it. Around Ponosevac, the place was covered with ammunition. Now, if you're asking for a specific place, I don't quite understand why. The point I'm making -- now, whether it's correct about the Geneva Conventions, I've already stated that I'm not an expert on the Geneva Conventions. Heavy calibre fire was poured against houses across Kosovo, and that has been made quite clear in my evidence and my reports that cover this entire area from early 1998 to 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Crosland, what would you say to me if I were to put it to you that among the equipment of the land forces, and therefore the Pristina Corps, in 1998 there were never any 40-millimetre calibre guns?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, you might be correct. There may not be 40. There may have been other calibres involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Beforehand we talked about rules, rules for using the army. Are you perhaps familiar with the rules for using anti-aircraft guns, Yugoslav made; 20-millimetre calibre and 30-millimetre Pragas, Czech made?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I'm not familiar, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. By your leave I would just like to say that these rules say that these weapons are used against individual weapons, mortars, machine-guns, infantry on the move, landing operations. All of that is contained in the rules. Not to refer to specific chapters and articles because I don't really want to waste time. So their use is not restricted only as an anti-aircraft weapon but it can also be used in land operations for targets from 1.500 to 2.000 metres.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If that's what you're stating is correct, sir then that is the rules which by you were playing.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement you also say that you know of the M-80 vehicle. On its turret it has a 20-millimetre gun. It's a caterpillar vehicle.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm -- I'm extremely familiar with it, sir, and there were caterpillar marks within metres of the Jashari family house in Donji Prekaze and the Likosane incidents, which I was one of the first people to go in and see. And also along with the caterpillar marks, as you quite rightly call them, the tracks, there were --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. I'm not talking about caterpillar marks. I'm talking about these weapons -- or, rather, artillery pieces. M-80 is not for anti-aircraft use; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think with any Armoured Personnel Carrier you can use it both in a land role and in an air role. That would be crazy not to use it against for air defence, a weapon of that ability.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Crosland. Could the Registrar please show us Prosecution Exhibit 2129. Mr. Crosland, on the screens in front us we should see your report of the 18th of May, 1998. It has to do with the village of Donji Obilic in the Drenica area.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With respect, sir, this is not my report. This is an ECM report from headquarters Sarajevo. If this is the one dated the 8th of May, time zone 08-05-18 17:52:01, that's not my report; that's from ECMM headquarters in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: But this report speaks of Kosovo. Could the Registrar control it down a bit? [In English] Scroll down please. Okay. [Interpretation] Since this was exhibited along with your own evidence, were you perhaps in this vehicle on the 11th of May in Donji Obilic, and were you stopped at a check-point by a 15-year-old boy armed with an AK47 rifle and wearing a flak jacket?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, with great respect I was stopped on many, many occasions and to ask me for one specific thing -- as I say, this report is not my report and if I was involved in this incident, then fine, but I have no -- unless there is a report of mine that confirms this then I can't really comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: You also spoke of the number of soldiers of the KLA. Do you perhaps know that a considerable member of -- number of members of the KLA were arrested and killed in the border belt and that all of these incidents were verified by mixed commissions of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and Albania?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, if I recall correctly, there was one very heavy engagement up on the -- I think near -- close to the Moranje [phoen] position. I didn't go to visit that one of the I was then shown pictures of another engagement in the area of Pastrik mountain and I was shown pictures of people of fighting age dressed in KLA uniform that had been killed whilst apparently coming across the mountains, but again we were not taken too this specific position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Were you aware, though, Mr. Crosland, that mixed commissions comprising representatives of the two governments of Yugoslavia and Albania did investigate killings in the border belt? Were you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It doesn't come readily to mind, Your Honour, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps remember that in the border belt, that is to say in the same situations where members of the KLA were killed and arrested, enormous quantities of weapons were ceased, an amount sufficient for arming a division. Perhaps you know of that? Would that perhaps jog your memory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, sir, there was one -- I believe one major occasion where a considerable number of KLA fighters were killed on the area. I think it was in the area of Moranje. The exact numbers and details of weaponry I don't -- I don't recall, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Several times you mentioned the personnel levels of the KLA. I would just like to know what your own estimate is. How many members of the KLA could have got killed during the fighting in 1998?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know is the honest answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could you perhaps tell us what the losses would have been percentage-wise compared to their personnel levels? Could you give us a percentage at least what the anticipated losses could have been?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I couldn't, no. But what I would say is that there were documents came from Serbia that indicated 688 were being liquidated. So I return the question to you, with great respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Crosland, I'm the one who is putting questions here, but let us support what you've said just now. Could the Registrar please show us 6D104.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is the purpose of this, Mr. Cepic?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you allow me, Your Honour, with your permission, of course, I would like to display the book that was published in Pristina 2002, "The Phoenixes of the KLA," listing over 600 names of fighters from different locations who were killed in 1998. So the sources from Pristina and Belgrade tally in terms of the approximate number of KLA members killed in 1998. That is to say precisely what Colonel Crosland said just now, over 600 fighters. Only in 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But the witness knows nothing about this. He's already made it clear, and all you're doing is engaging in a tit for tat contest by saying, oh, I can show you the source of that, but so what? We know it exists. Let's move to something the witness can deal with.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. This was just because the witness said that at that time in his view there were 400 fighters.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 30 of your statement, the army of Yugoslavia provided fire support to Western Kosovo from Decani, it was the army of Yugoslavia and the unit for special operations that were guarding the relevant artillery position. My question is whether you yourself saw that it was members of the unit for special operations guarding the artillery position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, we -- I physically went down to Visoko Decani, a very fine monastery that's on the right of the road, on the north side of the road. We then drove up towards the hotel and by some good luck or whatever we actually drove right through a six-gun artillery position and out the other side. In that position were both VJ and also JSO personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: As a soldier do you believe that the -- the army of Yugoslavia needed a police unit, a state security unit to guard its deployment lines?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, with respect that's a matter for the Vojska Jugoslavija. All I'm saying is that the internal situation, as I understand it, was a priority for the MUP in all its forms. That is something to do with the Yugoslavia constitution that has absolutely no dealing with myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Further on you say that in all the major cities in Kosovo there were joint bases of the MUP and the army, or they were just becoming joint bases. Did you mean the barracks of the VJ when you said that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In -- for instance, in Pec and Djakovica, and in Decani, as we've just spoken about, they appeared to be coming closer together. As I've tried to explain, I have no problem with and would expect if both forms of -- policing and military were working together, it makes perfectly good sense. But as I understand it the Vojska Jugoslavija under the Pristina Corps had certain bases --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I understand you. The specific question had to do with bases or barracks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I've said, during 1998, we saw, within what were initially VJ bases, MUP personnel and equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Crosland, did you perhaps know that in the barracks of the army of Yugoslavia throughout Kosovo 10 years prior to the period that you're testifying about facilities were built for housing members of the MUP who were on duty in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, with great respect, sir, I wasn't in Kosova at that stage, so I can only take your word for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 33 of your statement you talk about repainted vehicles. That is to say that you saw different vehicles of the army of Yugoslavia coloured into MUP colours from green to blue, BOV-3, BOV M, and so on and so forth. If equipment was given to the MUP by the army, do you know that it was done strictly through relevant state organs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, of course I don't know the answer to that. I'm just making a statement that equipment that -- that was not normal to the organisation of battle of the MUP was given additional equipment which came, I presume, from the Vojska Jugoslavija as it had a -- green paint underneath blue, as stated in paragraph 33.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know how many villages were there in Kosovo in 1998? Can you give me a ballpark figure at least?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would think several hundred. I mean, what -- what is classed as a village is a couple of -- two or three houses together or what? We tried to visit most of the area, and I would suspect there are several hundred villages, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: The areas that you visited most were Decani, Djakovica, and Pec, and this is where you observed damage in the villages. Wouldn't that be correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With respect, sir, that's not correct. We toured extensively from Kosovska Mitrovica across the northern route through Rudnik and Pec and all the villages there. We came across the Drenica complete. We drove many times from Pristina through the principal routes from Lapusnik, Komorane, to Klina and on to Pec. We then went down from Lapusnik through Malisevo, Rakovina -- sorry, through Lapusnik, through Malisevo to Orahovac and on to Djakovica. We came down from Klina along the Beli Drim past Rakovina into Djakovica. We also used to use the road from Pristina down to Stimlje, through Crnoljevo, Dulje, Blace, through Suva Reka, all over the Suva Reka area and the Pagarusa valley because of the IDP problem later in that year, on to Prizren; and we then came south through Urosevac through Strpci, Brezovica, the skiing areas, and down into Prizren. We then went west of Prizren down to Vrbnica, and from Zur we went all the way down to Brod and [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- as well as going on to the eastern side of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you're mostly talking about the western part of Kosovo. Do you know that in the course of 1998 from over 300 villages the KLA attacked villages, institutions, the MUP, the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think, sir, I've made that clear in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you also know that over 90 villages voluntarily returned weapons to the state institutions and those weapons had been previously given to them by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that specific fact, sir, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Just answer by yes or no. Do you know that the army of Yugoslavia never participated in any conflicts against the KLA around the town of Prilep, in any villages around the town of Prilep? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I made it clear that the firepower was used which came from the Vojska Jugoslavija. Whether they were physically on the ground or not is another matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now let's talk about the meeting which took place in Belgrade on -- on 17 October 1998 at the British embassy. You met with Mr. Drewienkiewicz, and you told him that there were two chains of commands in -- of command in Kosovo and that they were separate; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you make that statement, sir, then I don't necessarily dispute it. I presume you're talking about the VJ and the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Precisely, so. And this is what Mr. Drewienkiewicz said in paragraph 16 of his statement. If Mr. Drewienkiewicz states that, then we can consider it to be true. Isn't at that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, that's not my -- that's not my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's going to make our job a lot easier, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 48, you're talking about the border belt, and this is the belt which the task of protection of state borders applied, and this was to be done by the army. Can you just briefly explain what the border belt was, in keeping with international laws and regulations, and what are usually the authorities of the army in such a belt?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, I -- I've already stated that at the beginning of the conflict from what I understood by having been briefed by the FLS that the border -- the international border security was the remit of the Vojska Jugoslavija to a distance of 500 -- or maybe 2 kilometres. The border belt you refer to I assume you mean to the west of the Djakovica which is one of the key areas we've spoken about already from the influx of both men and material across that border into the Dukagjin area and on into the Drenica. And I think I've given credence to the fact that this was understandably one of the strategic areas that the Serbian security forces needed to try and control in order to limit the -- the men and material coming in for the UCK. So I hope I've answered your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Crosland. And now just to follow up on that. The Kosovo Verification Mission gave it -- gave its estimate on the 15th of March, or even earlier on in February of that year, having toured the border, having provided their analysis of the meeting in Rambouillet, and according to their estimate the army lacked some 2 or 3.000 soldiers and that number would have enabled them to perform the task properly. Would you agree with that estimate, that assessment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, I had detailed conversations with General Dimitrijevic [Realtime transcript read in error, "Drewienkiewicz"] that this border belt area between and Kosovo and that you could lose two or three brigades in a very mountainous area in an attempt to keep the border area secure, so I don't disagree with that estimate at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [In English] I think we have a mistake in transcript. Page 84, line 10, it is not General Drewienkiewicz; I think General Dimitrijevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And yesterday we heard that in paragraph 69 you stated that additional brigades of the VJ, the 211th and the 1st armoured brigade, were deployed in the area of Kursumlija, and another armoured brigade, probably the 37th brigade, was deployed in the area of Raska.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's -- sorry. I beg your pardon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Do you know where Kursumlija and Raska are?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I visited them on several occasions, sir, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Are they in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Raska is outside of Kosovo. Raska is north of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And Kursumlija?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Kursumlija is also outside of Kosovo. As I said yesterday, sir, it was one of the forward operating base.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Thank you. Since you were on the ground, and this was also stated by the Kosovo Verification Mission in their assessment on the 15th of March, 1999, do you know that the KLA activities escalated during the negotiations in France precisely at that time are you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we were all aware of that fact an extremely worried by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you also know that the Chief of the General Staff, General Perisic, in the course of 1998 on several occasions toured and controlled the -- the units that were deployed in Kosovo? I'm just going to say that this was in February, May, August, October, November 1998.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm well aware of that fact and one would expect a Chief of the General Staff to go and do a tour of his -- of his troops for all the obvious reasons, sir. I think I referred to that in my report at some stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you perhaps know that the commander of the 3rd Army at the time, and we're talking about 1998, and that was General Samardzic, was personally at the forward command post of the 3rd Army and that he spent there several months in Kosmet, in Pristina, between July and October 1998, and that he made daily decisions on the use of forces in Kosovo and he daily reported to General Perisic in Belgrade? Are you aware of all that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not specifically aware of that, sir, but I would entirely understand that that would be in accordance with normal military procedures.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Paragraph 64 of your statement, you're talking about the withdrawal of the Serb forces after the conclusion of the agreement with Holbrooke. In the case against Milosevic, on page 8041, you said that the VJ withdrew, that they retired to the barracks, and that you commended them for that act.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is entirely correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now we come to Podujevo. You say in your statement in paragraph 65, around the 19th or the -- 21 December you found a mixed battle group of VJ and MUP to the west of Podujevo. Do you know that immediately after the withdrawal of the Serb forces into Podujevo the KLA took the entire region west of Podujevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think so. I've already made that statement, and they came from the area of Bajgora which is further north-east up to Mitrovica, which was another known KLA area. I mean, as I've tried to explain, the situation was extremely flexible and it would -- people would take control of one area and then for various reasons would leave it, and the other side would come back in. And, yes, I accept what you say, sir, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: If you allow me, Your Honour, just one correction for the transcript. At page 86, line 17, "In the region of Podujevo," not just Podujevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Should that be "from the region of Podujevo?"

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: "From," exactly, Your Honour. Exactly, Your Honour. Exactly, Your Honour. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's withdraw from the region of Podujevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You also know that the KLA arrived in Lapastica, Gornja, Donja; Brusnik; and so forth, and that when this happened the entire non-Albanian population was expelled from that region of Podujevo; and also that there were frequent attacks on the Pristina-Nis road and that road is one of the most significant roads in Kosovo. Are you familiar with all that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I am. And I think I made it clear that this is your main supply route, as we call it, MSR, back to 3rd Army in Nis. And, again, it is of strategic importance to be held in a correct manner. I don't have any problem with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Can we now see Exhibit P680, please. Shortly, we will have a document before us. Can we please have page 2. This is a report of the Kosovo Verification Mission covering the period between 26 February and for March. At the top of the page -- [In English] [Previous translation continues].... [Interpretation] The KLA force in the Podujevo area managed to carry out an attack in the town itself effectively taking the town itself. Do you know in addition to attacks on civilians the KLA also attacked the town of Podujevo itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I've stated, sir, many areas changed hands many times, and this happened then. I know it was an area of major issue between the KLA and the Serbian security forces, as I think I made clear, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And the main stronghold of these force -- forces was in the villages Dobra, Bradas, Dobratin, west of Podujevo, and Gornja and Donja Lapastica. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wouldn't doubt that at all, sir, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: If I also say that the Kosovo Verification Mission never mentioned in any of their reports that those particular villages were razed, would you agree with that if I put it to you that way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir, because in paragraph 65 of the current report for this particular session, I state they did considerable damage to the villages west of Podujevo, Bradas, Dobratin, Gornja and Donja Lapastica.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: As a result of the fighting between the KLA and the Serb forces. Wouldn't that be correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It may well have been because of the fighting between the forces. It's the degree of damage that was done to the civilian environment. Whether it was KLA or civilian environment, that is for other people to decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, what you are saying was confirmed by Colonel Ciaglinski who mediated between the parties in the month of December, and he was awarded by a medal of the United Kingdom. His words were contrary to what you're saying now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I -- with respect, sir, I don't have his statement, and what you've said, there I wouldn't -- I disagree in content. But if that is a statement he has made, then I cannot possibly answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I thank you. When did you meet Colonel Lazarevic for the first time? Under what circumstances, to be more precise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't recall off the -- off the top of my head. I'm sorry. You have to remind me.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: If you'll allow me, in November 1998, the region of Dule, Colonel Lazarevic had called you because the terrorists had used hand rocket launchers. They attacked a column of the VJ army, that was not a combat volume couple. They killed four soldiers. They wounded four soldiers. And after that, you visited the outpatient surgery in Prizren where these wounded soldiers were brought to. Is that all correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, sir, for reminding me. If that was the -- I can't remember if that was the first time I met Colonel Lazarevic. But I had returned from Prizren that night and we got to the area Dulje Blace, and Colonel Lazarevic asked me to return with him had because of the incident you've just outlined. We did that. We went back with himself. He escorted himself into the hospital, where I sadly saw that one body of a VJ soldier was lying. I paid my respects to him. I then offered the entire contents of our medical pack. I've had medical training myself, but I said I'm sure there are doctors here who are better able to treat the four or five or six young soldiers, many of who were in shock. After that, we then sat down together and we made a joint statement, where I along with Colonel Lazarevic said that this was an illegal act by the KLA against the soldiers concerned, and that statement was sent back to the united kingdom. Where it went to, I don't know. And I totally agree with it. I would -- as a soldier, I am under duty under the Geneva Convention to offer help to any military person wounded in the course of actions, whether those actions are legal or illegal. And as a professional soldier that lost many people, we did that and helped as best we could.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
