utterances.text: Now that we're talking about Dulje, do you know that a combat group in keeping with the Sainovic-Naumann-Clark agreement was deployed on that road in order to secure the position and to be there to prevent frequent attacks by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Tell me what the relevance of that question is to the evidence that we're hearing from this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the witness is talking about the action in Racak, he's mentioning a unit that was nearby, and this was precisely the unit that I've just mentioned, Your Honour. And we can find this in his statement, paragraph 67, if my memory serves me well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's the relevance of your question? I mean, the witness has, throughout his evidence, told you of the many responsible things that the army of Yugoslavia were doing, and there were so many things that they were doing that were in keeping with military necessity, and many things were entirely reasonable. You don't have to prove that. He's conceded it all along.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So what is it? What is the point of the question, like so many of the others you've been asking recently?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was just to give the legitimacy to the unit that was in place, to say that nothing had been premeditated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He just told you it was an entirely legal attack on the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your leave, I'm talking about the 15th of January about Racak; and in paragraph 67, a mention is made by the VJ unit near Dulje. This is what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But what -- tell me the purpose of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The army did not participate in the operation in Racak, and nothing was planned at the corps level, especially not the operation in Racak as it is stated in the statement. It says that there is a close cooperation between the MUP and the corps, and headquarters was in Pristina. General Lazarevic was in command, and it was very clear that this was a coordinated action in order to clean the area of -- from the KLA. However, the truth is that that unit was the play -- deployed there in keeping with the previously mentioned agreement, and this is the point -- point that I'm making.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect, to try and help the situation, I am not stating and never have stated that the Vojska Jugoslavija unit based in Dulje was involved in the operation in Racak. I stated in my paragraph 67, in order to set the scene, that beyond Racak down towards Crnoljevo was KLA territory, and that Dulje was further up that mountainous road many times up which I travelled. Whether the operation was a joint operation or not, as I say to you there, I would be surprised if it wasn't. But if the learned gentleman says it was only a MUP operation, then so be it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I still don't understand what that question was about, I have to confess. It must be me.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, is this a convenient time for our break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I was hoping you would finish before the break, Mr. Cepic, but that's obviously not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Just a couple more questions, Your Honour, if you allow me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I was hoping you would focus your questions. Just let me find this again.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [In English] And if you allow me to say in the meantime, I made a mistake. I said agreement between Sainovic and Clark. It is not Sainovic, Milosevic and -- Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you know that their combat group was deployed on that road to secure the position because of frequent attacks by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That position was manned throughout the -- the Kosovo incident, and it also had been a long-time historical training area for the VJ, as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I still don't understand the purpose of the question, but you've answered it. And we will resume at 10 minutes to 2.00. We'll go into closed session while you leave the courtroom for the lunch break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber wishes to express its gratitude to everyone for -- for being so willing to continue the proceedings this afternoon in spite of the weather and in spite of the permission to leave. But we realise that it's important that we complete, if possible, the evidence of this witness today and the other witness proposed this week tomorrow. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just two questions very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Crosland, thank you. Very briefly, in October 1998, that is to say towards the end of the month, you, with the Canadian military attache and the assistant attache for defence of the USA, toured several barracks throughout Kosovo. You were in Urosevac, Pristina, and Prizren. In the barracks, you found units that were carrying out their regular duties, and you did not have any objections to raise during those visits; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that is correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Paragraph 75 of your statement speaks of the withdrawal of the units the army of Yugoslavia from Kosovo. You were there yourself, and you were following the withdrawal of part of the troops. My question is whether you know that during the withdrawal of the army units there was an attack by the KLA against these units, and on that occasion 36 soldiers of the army of Yugoslavia were abducted and killed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was aware, sir, that there was an attack and there was a fair degree of meddling by the KLA around Prizren, and I passed the message through various communications to Ramush Haradinaj that he had better understand and comply with the crease fire in order to allow Colonel Delic's brigade and about 5.000 or even 10.000 Serbs -- civilian Serbs to leave Prizren peacefully. I, in fact, was the last person out at the end of the convoy and ensured that the brigade and -- and all the Serbian civilians got safely to Brezovica and Strpce or wherever else they wanted to go. And I got Colonel Delic's formation into Pristina and then continue kind on to Podujevo, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel Crosland. That was my last question. Thank you to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cepic. Do you know that whether 36 soldiers were abducted and killed during that period.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not know of that number, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did you know of any, in fact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew there was -- excuse me, sir. I knew there was some killed in and around Prizren, and I also believe that I think one or two German troops were wounded. We did also thought it was urgent to get the medical supplies of the German unit in there to come and treat those who had been wounded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I want to make it, first of all, clear in the record that the Pavkovic Defence does not join Mr. Cepic with regard to the statement that everything DZ said is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Colonel, my name is John Ackerman. I represent General Pavkovic, and I have a lot of less questions to ask you than I thought I did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nice to hear, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We'll get through this as quickly as we can. I want to ask you about a matter that keeps coming up, and that is the -- the purported statement of General Ojdanic that force is to be met with force or force will be met with force. When dealing with terrorists, isn't that pretty much the standard operating procedure for the international community these days. Will you deal with terrorists, you meet force with force?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are various measures and levels of force, sir, that I think are appropriate, and it is one of the golf-clubs in the security forces army that should be used and used diligently and appropriately, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But what Ojdanic didn't say was force wouldn't be met with excessive force, he just said force would be met with force. That doesn't have any particular significance by itself, does it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not entirely, but that was not quite true of what was going on on the ground, as I have attempted to tell the Court during the course of these sessions, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to ask you a few questions about your testimony, yesterday. In your statement and in your testimony, yesterday, and even in a question from Judge Bonomy at page 50 of the transcript, you were talking about various key people that you were talking with that didn't seem to want to hear the things you were telling them about Kosovo. How did that manifest itself? Did they say don't tell me about that. I don't want to hear about that. Or was it a little more subtle than that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Is this with regards to the KLA, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. With regards to what the VJ was doing, in your observation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, with respect to those two questions, if it's with regards to the KLA --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It regards to the KLA, that's what -- not the KLA, I'm sorry. It's in regards to the VJ. I think your statement was when you would tell certain key people in Belgrade about what you'd observed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Paragraph 42, towards the end, or at the end of it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Well, that -- so that is the impression that I got when dealing with in particular General Ojdanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So there was no statement to you like, don't tell me about that, I don't want to hear about it. It was just an impression that you got?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You were asked about -- again, I want to go back to this meeting force with force. At page 54 yesterday, you said this: "The KLA had no answer to the heavier weapons that both the tanks, the multi-rocket launcher systems, and the artillery that was deployed against various positions primarily in the area of Junik and from a firing position at Bjelaca over to Suva Reka and other villages that came under attack," and then you said: "The KLA did not have any weapons that could match these at all." Now, wasn't that also the case when NATO started bombing Kosovo and Serbia? The Serbs didn't have any weapons that could match cruise missiles or cluster bombs or B2 stealth bombers or such weapons either, did they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour and sir, the point I was making at the time was that there was disproportionate force being used by the VJ against the KLA. If we want to widen the issue as to how I spoke yesterday about the Vojska Jugoslavija and the MUP preparing to defend themselves from probably an inevitable NATO assault, I think I gave quite a meaningful praise to the army of Yugoslavia in the way they -- they deployed. And I suspect that having put more troops in, whether it was to do a cleansing operation or whether it was to influence the NATO planners who at that stage I suspect were having to look at either an air operation or a ground operation, and if there were more ground forces within Kosovo the Vojska Jugoslavija, then inevitably there would be consequential casualties to both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, that's an interesting answer that you've given us, I think, on more than one occasion. And what I'm really interested in is the question that I asked and that was: The Serbs didn't have any weapons that would match cruise missiles, cluster bombs, B2 stealth bombers, weapons of that nature, did they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. They didn't, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ackerman, the witness has answered the question you asked in a way that has a relevance for our case. But if all you're doing is inviting an answer that compares NATO's conduct with the conduct of the VJ, according to the witness's evidence and that of others, then it is irrelevant to our case how NATO behave.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I totally agree with that and that isn't where I was going.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I can see it is relevant to certain issues and that's why I didn't interrupt you. But because you didn't like the witness's approach, which I think did credit to your question because it is a vague question otherwise, then I thought that perhaps that is what you were doing. But as long as it's not, then you can carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You've -- you've talk about this a number of times regarding that defence attache meeting, where you claim that Ojdanic was confronted with evidence regarding VJ activities in Kosovo. And I'd like you to take a look at P2554, if you will. And while that's coming up, you recall this morning that Mr. Sepenuk was asking you about that and more specifically about a statement apparently by you that General Ojdanic denied the use of VJ air assets against the KLA. Do you remember all of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I remember all of that, and I think I made the comment that I'd never implied that VJ air assets had been used in this particular campaign I said I'd seen MiGs coming off Pristina airfield, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. That's exactly what you said. I want to look at page 2 of this document, P2554. And if you look at paragraph 5, and it may be correct that this was not something that you had mentioned, but this report which I think is your report says: "During questions, Ojdanic categorically denied the use of VJ air for" something "ops." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, beg your pardon, sir. It's still flashing around -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It should be on the screen there, right there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes, I can see that, sir. As I've already stated, I've never, never initiated, as far as I understand, anything about air ops in this particular campaign.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, is this a report that you submitted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I -- sir, without looking at the top, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Let's look at the first page, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's signed by Ambassador Donnelly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Oh, it's a Donnelly report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So I'm afraid it's not my report, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would he have gotten that information from you regarding that meeting of defence attaches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He would have got that view from me, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, there were some questions also this morning about the videotape that you now say was turned over to Colonel Jovanovic. Have you ever seen -- that's the tape I take it that was made by your warrant officer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct. I believe so, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: My question is have you ever seen that tape in any of your meetings with the OTP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, who is the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Office of the Prosecutor, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Forgive my ignorance, sir. I have not seen it since the day I passed it across to the Vojska Jugoslavija.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did they ever ask you to get it for them, the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not as far as I'm aware, sir, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You told us that, to your knowledge, a copy was also delivered to your ministry. Do you know if the Prosecutor ever requested it from them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know, is the correct answer, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to go to a different subject with you now. You allude to this in one of your reports, but I don't want to bring up the report and spend the time it would take to find it. You spent a lot of time in the Balkans and in Serbian and Kosovo. I think you learned to speak Serbian language; and from your statements, it's clear that you gained some important and lasting impressions about the situation there and the people there. I'm interested in your explanation of what you learned about the people and the cultural attitudes that persisted during your time there. For instance, what did you find particularly striking about what you described as the clan-based society of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By that, you were meaning the clan-based society of the Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was an interesting format for families, perhaps something which we could all learn by in keeping our families together, rather than separating them with the inevitable conferences that brings. The patriarchal effect, again, I think is a positive effect. It may not go down very well in today's dual society, but I think possibly we could learn something from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And was there some historical and cultural view of revenge that you learned about, about the necessity -- the acceptability and even the necessity of the concept of revenge and taking revenge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There is the honour feud and the blood feud, and that was, as I understand it, taken very seriously, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that's very different from the kind of cultural thinking we have in the West, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is extremely different. But as I've travelled the world, I think it behooves us to try and understand the situation in which we are operating and not to apply purely Western or international conditions to the operational area. One must take both the good parts and the bad parts of the area you're working in and try to understand them, apply oneself, and see it from their point of view. After all, it is their country.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. And in your statement of June 2006, at paragraph 49, you talk about this blood vengeance, and you say this that "in the Balkans the man with the biggest stuck won and it's always been like that."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think, with respect, it does appear to be like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The United Kingdom has gone round the world beating the hell out of most people starting with the crusaders, and so on. So I will hold my hand up as being guilty, as well of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The same as the occasional American?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We do that as well, sir, for which I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You don't need to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We've forgotten that a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In your October statement, the one that we're primarily using here, paragraph 56 -- yeah, it is paragraph 56, you speak of your report of 6 November 1998 regarding conversations with Dimitrijevic. And one of the things he will told you he was concerned about, and I think this came up yesterday, was with the withdrawal of VJ/MUP forces the KLA was quickly occupying those locations. And what he said to you his concern was that if this continued, he would concerned that MUP would forcefully react to that, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is absolutely correct, sir. And that statement was passed on directly to my own Ministry of Defence, and I'm sure they got in touch with allied headquarters around the world who were dealing with this problem because it was, as I've said already, a very genuine [Realtime transcript read in error "general"] concern and had happened on more than one occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, you also say there that he told you another concern that he had was the 3rd Army commander General Pavkovic might also react without permission from the General Staff and outside the military chain of command; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, if we look at --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The transcript --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: 102, 23, the witness I believe said an a very genuine concern, and it says a very general concern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to look at P684. It's a sitrep, I believe, a report of this meeting. And if we look at page 2, what this contemporaneous report indicates, regarding what Dimitrijevic said at that time, was: "He also indicated that the 3rd Army commander may also react without permission from the General Staff." You see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's -- if you're referring to the bottom of paragraph 4, yes,, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It doesn't say 3rd Army commander Pavkovic, just that the 3rd Army commander may also react without permission from the General Staff, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would be quite in order for the field commander to react, as appropriate, as a field commander. I don't have any problem with that. That would be normal military procedure. Sorry, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But what it's saying without permission from the General Staff, and bear in mind we're talking about November 1998 here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a very difficult time, sir, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. It was also a time when the 3rd Army commander was General Samardzic, not General Pavkovic, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're quite right there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So when you say in your statement that what he said was he was concerned that 3rd Army commander General Pavkovic might react without permission from the General Staff, either you're wrong about what he said or he was wrong. Which is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think what has been muddled up here is that General Pavkovic was then the head of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And the immediate operational unit headquarters within that area. So there is an error there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, then there's I think a similar error in paragraph 57 where you say: "It was apparent in the aftermath of the Racak incident on 15 January 1999 that Pavkovic was clearly the field commander for Kosovo operations." Do you know by 15 January 1999 Pavkovic was the 3rd Army commander and no longer in the field in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I -- I take your point as -- as a definitive point. I mean, as commander of 3rd Army ultimately he is responsible for the actions of his army whether he's the immediate commander in the field which I think by then was General Lazarevic, I accept that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your same statement, paragraph 53. You talk about a conversation with Dimitrijevic on the 3rd of October where he talked about the use of heavy weapons, and he said something to you along the line that he thought General Pavkovic was trying to make his name, and what you say in that paragraph is implicit within that was the intention to suppress the KLA and the Kosovo Albanian population. When you say it was implicit in that statement, what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That, sir, was my impression of the expression of General Dimitrijevic at that -- at that particular meeting and therefore the impression that I gain. Now, one can argue if that impression was right or wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah, I think one can, because one possibility is that General Dimitrijevic was telling you that because he believed it. The other possibility is he was telling you out of some kind of petty jealousy or some effort to deflect attention from his own role.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I -- I can't answer that question, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I know you can't. At this same meeting, you also indicated that Dimitrijevic seemed to indicate, and the words seemed to indicate are of interest to me, that General Pavkovic would again stray, again stray, from the military chain of command and react to orders or indications from Belgrade. First the qualifying language seemed to indicate apparently he didn't directly say that to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think my only comment on this, sir, is that this meeting I think it was held in the FLS offices which I presume things were taped, not to put too fine a point on it, that I don't think General Dimitrijevic would say something that he didn't think was correct. It's a very brave statement to have made from a man who was quite clearly or should have been clearly at the centre of operations in an insurgency operation at chief of counter-insurgency.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That seems to me less than something saying directly that he believed General Pavkovic would again stray from military chain of command am I right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, sir that is my impression that I gained from this particular meeting sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you claim that -- that these words again stray from the military chain of command may have been said, and I want to ask you this: Do you have one concrete bit of evidence, one document, anything of that nature that shows that General Pavkovic ever strayed from the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All I'm reporting, sir, is what came out of various meetings that General Dimitrijevic with the ambassador as is stated if paragraph 54.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So your full knowledge is what you're being told by Dimitrijevic and maybe Perisic on occasion; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know that there was jealousy going on in the General Staff at that time because in some person's view Pavkovic had been promoted before he should have? Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did -- I did hear information to that -- to that effect, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you certainly know don't you that General Perisic as Chief of the General Staff would have removed Pavkovic from any post if he'd not been following the chain of command or following orders or operating outside the chain of command he certainly could have done that couldn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I presume he could have whether he had to approach President Milosevic I would not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you had no indication did you that Perisic ever tried to remove Pavkovic from any of his posts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not as far as I'm aware sir no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And in view of the kind of thinned that Perisic and Dimitrijevic were telling you about Pavkovic, would you be surprised to learn that at the same time he said these things to you he ordered a certain of merit in June 1998 to General Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think if I remember correctly, sir, there were quite a few certificates handed out at that particular stage, which I think is understandable to keep morale at a high level and reward good work, I understood, that the Vojska Jugoslavija and MUP were doing in Kosovo. And I think I understand that and tried to report in a fair and proper manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you believe that General Perisic as head of the General Staff, believing that as he told you General Pavkovic was operating outside of his orders and outside of the chain of command and in violation of all the rules and regulations of the Yugoslav Army would at that time I'll ward him a certain of merit was that the kind of person you knew as General Perisic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, General Perisic appeared to me to be a very genuine person. He certainly had a lot of experience being the Chief of the General Staff I think it's impertinent for me to say whether General Perisic would issue a certificate or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you have any information about whether he did issue such certificate to General Pavkovic? If you do I can show it to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, I -- I don't know. It's not my -- any of my business to be honest.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I'm interested now in your statement of December of 2000, in paragraph 2 you said this: "When Perisic was the Chief of the General Staff of the VJ, the VJ kept largely to its constitutional tasks of security of the borders of the FRY," and you used the word constitutional task. And then when you testified in the Milosevic case, at page 8024 you said this to Mr. Milosevic: "Under your constitution, Mr. Milosevic, the VJ had a priority to protect the national border and 500 metres, and that was written down in the constitution." My question is where did you get this information about this being in the constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was what I understand was the briefing that I was given when I joined as the defence attache in Belgrade from the FLS, because one was keen to understand what the-the constitutional position of the Vojska Jugoslavija was in attempting to understand the -- the whole situation, you know, within Yugoslavia and within the Balkans as a whole, as it was quite clear that one had joined a station that -- a country that was still in turmoil after Dayton, and there was a good chance that further developments would occur, which sadly has happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did anyone ever show you what they claimed was a provision of the constitution in this regard, to show you the constitutional provision you were being told --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not as far as I'm aware, sir, no. I think it was a -- just an informal briefing in FLS as to, you know, how the various forces of Yugoslavia were integrated and frankly it was out of interest in my own side to say what is the Vojska Jugoslavija and the Ministry of Interior which is of -- as I say of genuine interest, and I think as a defence attache one should you know understand the workings of the various forces that might be deployed in an internal situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would you accept if I represent to you that there is absolutely nothing in the constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia that talks about the VJ's priority to parole text the national borders or about a 500 metre border belt or anything like that, absolutely nothing? Would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as I say, sir, I've just said -- said that is what I was told by the FLS.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you never -- you never checked to see if that was correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't -- I didn't physically check, no. I accepted the briefing I was told because it was part of the in-briefing that went to all attaches so they understood where and how far -- how close they could go to borders, for instance, without causing alarm on the -- or not -- in the FRY at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to suggest to you that what you were told by General Perisic and General Dimitrijevic about that was absolute little false and we'll go into some of that as we go forward here. At paragraph 48 of your October 2006 statement you say this: "By the sum of 1998 the then 52 corps commander General Pavkovic began to operate outside the constitutional tasks" again you said constitutional tasks, "by involving the VJ in operations against the KLA in the interior of Kosovo." Now, where did you get this information? Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as I've just explained you, sir, those were the -- the -- the parameters of what I was told when I joined the FLS. I can only repeat that to you. If that is not the case, then I was falsely informed. .

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When you joined the FLS you were told that in the summer of 1998 General Pavkovic began to operate outside the constitutional task by involving the VJ in operations against the KLA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, with respect sir when I joined as a defence attache in August or September 1996 --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I want to know with your got this information.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Bit summer of 1998. Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've just stated there that's because of the briefing I received when I first joined, and then when the situation developed I was told that their constitutional tasks were the border security, varying in distance as appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So in the summer of 1998 somebody told you that General Pavkovic was operating outside the constitutional tasks as you said here. Somebody must have told you that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as a -- I've already made clear this -- these were meetings we had with General Dimitrijevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Who indicated this. Now, whether he was indicating this true or false, I only report what I was told.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you know that at that time, the summer of 1998, General Pavkovic's superior was General Samardzic of the 3rd Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you see any orders from Samardzic to Pavkovic regarding the use of the VJ during the summer of 1998? Yeah, 1998.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'd been very surprised if I had seen any orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. You've never seen any?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I would think these are classified information.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you investigate to see if there was any truth to the statement that Pavkovic was operating outside his constitutional tasks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, as I've stated on several occasions, on meetings when this information was passed to me it was obviously of extreme interest for our intelligence and analysis back home to put it together as you're well aware having had military background yourself coming from all sources. Now, I'm one source. I think you've had some background, sir. If not, I may be mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, you're not, but I don't know how you knew that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that's good intelligence, sir. But the point I am making is that if you were in a position as the defence attache, you are expected to keep both your eyes and ears open, and information coming from such a senior person such as General Dimitrijevic or even senior such as General Perisic that there are problems in the army chain of command I would submit to the Court and to your good self that that is of extreme interest to one's own intelligence at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No doubt --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now whether -- I beg your pardon for interrupting you. No doubt whether that is true or false, I as a source will say that. I'm sure as we all know we're all bugged and on closed circuit cameras from every angle we are at, someone else will come up with either a correct assessment or an incorrect assessment. Now, as far as I'm aware, and I can stand to be corrected there obviously, that statement was never challenged by my intelligence services.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You've got me focused on your good intelligence, and it makes me stand here and wonder what else you know about me, and I don't want you to answer that question. Okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay, sir, no problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Paragraph 48.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: General Dimitrijevic and Perisic implied to me on a number of occasions that they disagreed with the VJ being used on internal security operations and that General Pavkovic was bypassing the proper chain of command." Now, again you're using a kind of qualifying word that they implied to you. Did they directly tell you this or was this something that you just sort of concluded from some rather vague language of theirs? ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not at all sir. Again, as I have just explained, I mean, if you got two extremely senior and intelligence related generals telling you that they are unhappy about something going on, then either they are slinging in a real fast ball to try and unsettle the other side, or they are extremely concerned about the situation. And as you've indicated in the previous statement that there was some internal unrest at senior level about various people being promoted, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now, I think -- I shouldn't say this. Even with our own General Staff I am sure there are agitations between the various senior officers concerned as to who is getting more influence in -- in -- in current operations than he or she should be, and that --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I can't imagine an army where that is not true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't indeed, no. But as I say part of my job was to report back any instances which in all good faith were told to me on -- as I said on several occasions here by two very senior people which were obviously of extreme interest to our intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Colonel, it's very clear to me what I've heard from you in this courtroom and from your history that I've been able to read that you have a very good and logical mind, and it seems to me that if we apply some logic to this situation that the first thing we have to realise is that the proposition that Pavkovic was going around the chain of command and dealing directly with Milosevic makes no logical sense for a lot of reasons, one of which we've discussed and that would be the ability of Perisic to fire him. But the other one -- the other ones, clearly Milosevic could order Perisic to order Samardzic to order Pavkovic to do anything he wanted because he was the commander-in-chief of that military, and Perisic would be bound to follow those orders or resign, I take it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as you well recall, sir, that is one of the statements that I managed to get the late President Milosevic to admit to, that he was actually the commander in chief, and therefore ultimately responsible for the actions of the forces that were involved in this particular campaign. .

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, with --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But I don't -- excuse me. I do not -- I accept the chain of command you've outlined there is entirely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, if he was the commander-in-chief within the Supreme Defence Council, then the orders came from him down through Perisic, down through Samardzic down to the Pristina Corps if they had anything to do with the Pristina Corps. That would have been the chain of command it would make no sense for him to go around the chain of command and direct Pavkovic to do something when he had a chain that he could work through would it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wouldn't disagree with it, sir. That is why when I was approached by these two gentlemen I was approached by them on this occasion and they made this statement -- I mean, it is an incredibly serious statement to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And I -- if you're saying it was a smokescreen statement, then fair enough. That's -- that is a judgement that I cannot -- I only -- I cannot make. As I said already, a statement made to me like that needs to be reported back to my senior command for them to apply other sources that might or might not reciprocate and understand the -- the importance of this statement. But as far as I know, I was -- I was never contradicted per se.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'd like the usher to come and pick up a little me I have some documents that I have in it I'm going to ask you to refer to and it's much easier than to try to fine the correct pages on the screen and while that is being taken to you I would like you to look at a document that is not in there and that is 4D138. Are we getting the document? Yes, we are. We need the English version, please. Go to the next page, please. What we are looking at, Colonel, are the rules of service of the Yugoslav Army that went into effect in 1996 and were in effect, as I understand it, in 1998, the summer of 1998. And if we can enlarge paragraph 473 at the bottom. Now, these -- these rules of the VJ, 473 provides this: "Army units may be used to combat outlawed, sabotage, terrorist and other armed enemy groups," and then it has a "or" and we can skip that. "The chief --" we just lost it for some reason. "The chief the General Staff shall issue the order for the use of army units to carry out the task stated in this item." You see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do, sir, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That seems to indicate that the Chief of the General Staff can issue an order to use the army against terrorist activity without any constitutional authority or anything like that, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is -- that is quite clear, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But my point is I'm not actually against what you're saying. It's -- it's the way that things unfolded within Kosovo and primarily the -- the initial contact in 1998 with three MUP killed at Rudnik and there was a MUP reaction to that. Now, I was led to believe by FLS or whatever that the primacy for internal situations was with the MUP. Now, this appears to be at odds with what is stated here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Carter?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Respectfully, Your Honour, I'm concerned that this line ever questioning is going to directly to the objections that were being raised from the Defence yesterday. This witness cannot be deemed an expert on the law of the army of Yugoslavia or the defence of Yugoslavia or the individual constitution of the former Yugoslavia unless we would caution Defence in regards to the questions that he intends to elicit on these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The witness has made a statement that says that the army was acting outwith its constitutional rule without having had the opportunity of seeing the provisions which might define its rule, and he's now being shown documents which may be open to interpretation but do make statements about the role of the army. That seems to us to be entirely legitimate cross-examination on the statement given. He's not being asked to give expert testimony at all. So I repel that objection. Carry on, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Colonel, you've now -- you've now seen that. I now want you to look at one of the documents that I have given you and we can also put it up on the screen. It's 4D137, and Mr. Sepenuk showed this to you earlier today, a part of it. Now, you'll notice, I think, that this document is dated 28 July 1998.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And this morning your attention was brought to some parts of it. The -- the -- if you look, you'll see that it's a directive signed by General Perisic on July 28, 1998, at around the same time he was telling you that using the army away from the border belt was in violation of the constitution. You'll see his directive the preamble says to deploy the Yugoslav Army for securing state border with Albania units and facilities in the area of Kosovo and Metohija and to crush the armed rebel forces. And then if you go to the second page, the Yugoslav Army's deployment so far, that means what have we done up to the 28th of July, 1998, he says this: "Through its presence and by carrying out the training in the entire territory of Kosovo and Metohija, the army has had a repelling effect with regard to the Siptar terrorist forces and have offered direct assistance to the forces of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia." And then if we go then to the next page, it speaks about his directive regarding the engagement of the Yugoslav Army, at the very top of that third page he says: "Through quick actions coordinated with the force of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia, overwhelm and destroy the sabotage and terrorist forces in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija as per a special order from the General Staff of the Yugoslav Army." And you'll see that same language then under the tasks of the 3rd Army about halfway down the page. Now, does this seem a bit of a contradiction from a general who is telling you that you can't use the army this way at the same time he's ordering the use of this the army in this way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, with respect I go back to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: A moment, Mr. Crosland.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The document being shown is a directive. It is a contingency plan to be used at some later stage if it appears that there is a triggering event. That's the way this question is being --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's testimony that's not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're now giving evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Respectfully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You cannot object on the basis that you will explain what answer he ought to give that's a quite inappropriate way to interrupt. Now, what is it you are saying.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Respectfully, Your Honour the way this last question was asked was that this was an order that on one hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It was what directive was used throughout I've noted in my note here that's how it was put.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object very strongly to this objection she's telling the witness how to answer questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just hold on a second, please. In closed session. The witness will leave the courtroom and I'll deal with this now in his absence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Crosland, I'll remind you of the question in a form which I think cannot be disputed, and that was having read the document, do you agree that it seems a bit of a contradiction for that to be set out in a document by a general who says you can't use the army in this way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, my only comment is that, as I made clearly throughout my statement, was that there was a denial, if that's not too strong a word, that there'd ever have been joint MUP and VJ operations. It was a surprise to me as a military man that that was a case, and that was what kept coming out from the briefings by the FLS and General Ojdanic. The fact that it was laid out in a document that's been issued here, I don't find peculiar at all, but that was the cut of the various intelligence briefings we were given. And when we pointed out the VJ and the MUP were acted together, this was categorically denied, if that's not too strong a term.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In your conversations with General Perisic, where he was intending to you that Pavkovic was using the army illegally and going around the chain of command and this was unconstitutional, did he ever tell you that he had issued a directive of this nature in July of 1998 or give you an idea of what that was? Or did he ever show it to you, or did General Dimitrijevic ever show it to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not aware that he ever did, sir, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Now, if you look at the very last page of this, I think you'll notice that it was distributed to the 3rd Army. Do you notice that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is 125, is it, at the back? Side flash 125, or P125 it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 25, 125. I don't know. The last --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The document you're looking at is 137, and the page I'm referring you to is actually page 7 of that document, I think, where it shows the distribution -- actually, it's page 6. At the bottom, it says: "Printed in seven copies and then submitted to," and then it says --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologies, sir. I see what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: "Copy to the 3rd Army command," see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand and see what you are showing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I just be clear about your last answer, two answers go. Why was it a surprise to you that there were any joint operations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. It was a surprise to me that there were not joint -- there shouldn't be joint operations, and yet we were told there were not joint operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think there may be a mistake in this transcript then. Just give me a second. Ah, yes. I hadn't read the entire answer. Thank you. It is clear. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The next thing that -- that we might consider, Colonel, is whether this directive of -- of General Perisic that was sent to the 3rd Army was ever acted on by the 3rd Army, and what I'd like you to do now is look at 4D140, which is I think 140 in your packet there. I think you'll see that what this is is now an order -- Your Honours have seen this earlier, of course. This is dated the next day, 29 July 1998, and this is an order; not a directive, but an order, signed by General Samardzic of the 3rd Army. And you'll notice on page 13 that copy one goes to the Pristina Corps command. And I suggest to you that what this is an order from General Samardzic to the Pristina Corps command, among others, implementing the directive from General Perisic and, in fact, using nearly identical language from what General Perisic used. If you look at page 7 -- page 6, it assigns unit tasks; and then 5.1, to the Pristina Corps; and then at the top of page 7, it says: "Launch rapid and energetic attacks in coordination with Serbian MUP forces to smash and destroy the terrorist forces in the zone of responsibility in accordance with my special order." And I think all I really want to ask you about is, do you understand this is an implementation by General Samardzic of the directive from General Perisic the next day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, yes. With respect, it is the classical staff dissemination of orders down the chain of command, which one would have expected in an army of the experience of Vojska Jugoslavija and a very interesting document to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And if you look at page -- page 6, about halfway down, there's a kind of small heading that says "Standby." And it seems to indicate that 6th August at 0500 is the -- is the starting off point for destroying the DTS which is the terrorist forces in accordance special order. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I see that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that's why I referred to the VJ and MUP early -- late August or late summer, early August -- early autumn deployment. So that is in line with what I have reported.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But it is not in line with the proposition that General Pavkovic was going outside that chain of command. These seem to be documents fully within the chain of command directing activity that Perisic -- that Perisic and Dimitrijevic were telling you was not proper.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I -- I fully accept that, sir. All I'm -- I will repeat is that when two senior generals of that nature make that comment to me, as a defence attache, I think it's only right and proper that I report it up the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Of course, it is; that's your job. All right. Now I want to go to something else. This -- this issue of how many KLA there were keeps surfacing as we go through your testimony, and my colleagues have brought up, even the Judge brought up various other information we've received during the course of this trial, regarding numbers that are dramatically larger than -- than what you've told us. And you keep telling us that -- that those numbers don't match what you were able to see on the ground in Kosovo, and I think maybe you and I can agree that there's a way to understand what you're saying. When you're dealing with terrorists, Colonel, terrorists are not like a conventional army. They don't gather together in barracks. They don't march around on parade grounds. They don't always go around wearing uniforms and carrying their weapons and looking like an army. I think it's the case, and I think you'll agree with me, that terrorists can only succeed by blending into the population, by making themselves basically invisible except on those occasions when they launch an attack, and then they go right back to invisibility again. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think this is some of the advice that I gave to General Dimitrijevic at the start of this particular campaign, that as I said, the goldfish in the bowl would be the Serb and the Serb forces within Kosovo in amongst a huge Albanian population. So I would agree entirely with what you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So it would be a virtually impossible task to stand on the ground in Kosovo and count the KLA, because that -- how would you know which guy you're looking at is a KLA and which one isn't. And like you said yesterday, I think you said yesterday, the one to tell us how many fighters there were in the KLA would be the KLA, and I think that was a fair statement on your part. Right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That, I believe, was the gist of the conversation, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah. Now, in the Milosevic -- I'm going to a different subject again. In the Milosevic trial at page 7962, you were talking about the general tactics that were being used by the Serbian security forces. I can tell you that many villagers from Kosovo, who have testified here, have talked about shells being fired over the tops of their villages. And I think this matches up with what you said in your statements here and in Milosevic where you said, "It appeared that on most operations, warning shots would be fired into the area of the villages that were about to be assaulted presumably to try and warn the civilian population that worse was to come." Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I think you even told us yesterday that -- that one sort of notable feature of this was that it appeared that it was -- that it was successful, that the civilians did leave the villages because virtually no one -- no civilians were killed in these -- these kinds of attacks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. That's as I understand it, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And so I think it would be fair to say that the target of these attacks was the KLA, not the Albanian people.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, with respect, sir, to that, you know, why was there so much collateral damage done post the assault or during the assault and laying waste of all the market areas in Pec, Decani, Djakovica, to name but three, and Urosevac, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I do understand your testimony about that, that your contention is that there was quite a bit of damage done that certainly had an effect on the people. But in terms of directly attacking the people of Albania, I think it's your opinion you didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think that's, with respect, sir, is a very large question. I mean, the psychological damage by warfare is a huge and ongoing business as we see every day in Iraq and Afghanistan, and that shells flying over villages against unarmed civilians in the majority, whether they were supporters of the KLA or not, I don't think is really the correct way to carry out these type of operations, in my -- in my opinion, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, that is -- that's, of course, an absolutely astute observation, and it's what we see, as you said, in Afghanistan and in Iraq and in all recent conflicts that we're familiar with, especially with a kind of weapon which that's being used these days. I want to go to -- if you want to comment on that, please free. I think that's what you were telling us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, sir, yes. The key to winning a counter-insurgency situation is winning the hearts and minds, and then providing the infrastructure for the civilian population, as I said, to get on with their daily life of making business, crops, farming, et cetera. And unfortunately most of the businesses, the crops, and the farms were burnt, razed to the ground throughout many, many areas of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I've just got a few more things I want to discuss with you, not much more left here. In your June statement of 2006, that's the one you made with regard to the Haradinaj case, you said this: "It was at one occasion pointed out to me that I should consider the focus of my interest better during my time in the Balkans," and then you said after that, "I always tried to report objectively that there was a growing terrorist problem in Kosovo. It was a regular occurrence that MUP officers and others were being killed by KLA. This was not good for the stability in the area." Now, when you say it was pointed out to you that you should consider the focus of your interest better, are you saying that you were being criticised for objective reporting about the KLA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could get into an awful lot of trouble over this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, wait a minute.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Go on, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's nobody's -- it's nobody's desire to get you into trouble, so we can do a thing called private session where nobody only the people in this room will hear your answer. Would you like to do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I'm quite happy to accept the brick bats. I always have. That's probably why I was five foot eight and now I'm five foot six. There was a -- a general misunderstanding about matters Balkans, I would say, throughout the international community. And it's very easy, as I said to many people, to view the civil war that had been going on in the Balkans since 1991 in Bosnia and Croatia and Slovenia and other places on the break-up of the former Yugoslavia. And I reminded people on several accounts that the civil war in the United Kingdom in 1642 took brother against brother, and probably one of the worst civil wars was the civil war in your country, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And that was probably only about 150 years ago. In the country of Holland, in which I now sit, the 100 years war and the wars of Orange and so on were also very bloody. And part of my attempt was to understand and to report in a correct manner and, as I think I have tried to suggest to the Court today, to understand the situation that the Vojska Jugoslavija in particular was in in Kosovo and to report in a fair and firm way. And where I understood there to be reason to -- to query and to question why very heavy firepower was being used - because I didn't consider this right against primarily a civilian population, albeit maybe with leanings towards or even tacit support for the terrorist organisation, I was one of the few people who would call it a terrorist organisation - I made it clear to the Vojska Jugoslavija that I was more than unhappy with that being used. At the same time, I made it very clear to many senior people that there was a huge amount of provocation being absorbed by both the VJ and the MUP, and that many brave and distinguished officers and men had been killed by the KLA. And they were having, as my army has over the century have, to accept that you are an army the political scenario and arm of the political wing. I still think there is a misunderstanding about the situation within the Balkans and there is an attempt to make it either a black or white scenario, when we know in most the world most areas are grey. The current situation in Kosovo I think leads to grave concern. And I know from my contacts still back in Belgrade that there is not only concern, there is a great fear that Veliki Albania may well take shape if - and I stress the if because I'm not in touch with what is going on in Pristina - Pristina or Kosovo becomes a protectorate or another state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand your concern, Mr. Crosland, but it's an area into which we dare not go. Our problems are big enough dealing with 1999 and --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- to some extent 1998.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Colonel, I want to ask you briefly about a report by Ambassador Donnelly. It's P683. I don't think you have it in that booklet there, but it will come up on the screen. And you'll recognise that it's a report about that meeting with Dimitrijevic in October, early October. The report's dated 3 October 1998.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. It is -- excuse me. It is from the ambassador, right, as you said so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. If you look at paragraph 4 -- and you were at that meeting, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I believe I was, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you look at paragraph 4, the ambassador says: "Dimitrijevic said that it seemed to him that the decision to punish the FRY had already been made." This was as early as October of 1998 he was saying that; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That, as it's stated there, is correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. What I want to ask you about, if we go to page 3, in paragraph 12, where the ambassador puts in his comments, he said about halfway down: "The expressed belief that the die is already cast is partly true [Realtime transcript read in error "through"]"? Now, is he saying there that Dimitrijevic is right, that the decision to punish the FRY had already been made, and that what followed in Rambouillet was just a sort of circus to set things up for NATO attack? Is that what he's saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With respect, sir, I did not go to Rambouillet, and I did not have anything to do with it. And I think to ask me to comment on what Ambassador Donnelly said is inappropriate, if I may say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I'll totally respect that. Colonel, thank you. I doesn't think I have any more questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave I have been mentioned by my learned friend, Mr. Ackerman. Actually, in relation to what the gentleman said, I claim that what we put to the witness is something from another witness's statement does not mean that our Defence supports that statement or, rather, that we accepted it. We would have challenged it during the cross-examination if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that, Mr. Cepic. The matter was dealt with lightly when it happened, and it didn't commit you to anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. [In English] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is a typo in the transcript that's just at the top of the screen. Line 132 -- page 132 line 4, I believe it should be "partly true," not "partly through. " I just thought I would catch that while it's still within our purview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr Crosland, my name is Dragan Ivetic, and I am one of the attorneys for Mr. Sreten Lukic. And I would ask you to pay close attention to my questions and try to limit yourself to answering just those questions, so we can try and move as quickly as possible through the testimony here today.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good day, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I believe you've already stated that in 1998 during your appointment as Defence attache to the UK embassy in Belgrade, that you did not have any accreditation with the Ministry of Internal Affairs of the Republic of Serbia. I want to just clear things up with you. During any of the time that you were in Yugoslavia, is it correct to say that you never had any accreditation status with the MUP of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had never had any accreditation, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you and can we conclude from that the fact that neither in your preparation for your assignment or deployment nor in the course of your deployment did you have any formal instruction, training or otherwise on the organisation, structure, or functioning of the Ministry of Internal Affairs of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think what you are saying is I wouldn't know anything about it. That is not correct. I made it my business to find out which -- the various organs of the MUP, as I've said already, when the operation started in Kosovo, it was quite clear that it would be a joint operation and, therefore, I needed to understand, as best as possible, between the various nuances of the MUP, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I appreciate that, sir. I think my question asked about formal instruction or training. Am I correct that you did not any formal instruction or training and all the acts undertaken were acts on your own to try and learn as much as you could?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Is it correct that you did not have any substantial or official contact with the MUP leadership in Belgrade or the most senior MUP officers on the ground in Kosovo during the time of your deployment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As you're well aware, sir, there are numerous defence and national days and other opportunities where the diplomatic corps, as a whole, gets together. And being an inquisitive person, I suppose, I would try and get into conversation with some of the more senior gentlemen. Sometimes they would they would chat on an interested basis, because of my background and sometimes they wouldn't, but I am -- it was social contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think you've answered my next question. You said there was a social contact. You never had any official contact meetings or contact, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mean, there were several high powered murders during our time there, which had political innuendo which would be discussed within the -- the embassy. And, obviously, I would listen to the conversations that accrued around these incidents, as I say, to understand fully or more fully the whole political and military picture of Yugoslavia as it then was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Am I correct that you would not consider yourself versed or an expert in the functioning structure, authority, or duties of the MUP staff in Pristina during 1998 or 1999?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. They kept themselves very much to themselves. I think from time to time I may have had the odd conversation with Andjelkovic and people to do with civil order within Pristina itself, again, as part of the overriding wish to find out what was going on in order to report fairly and firmly to my superiors.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You say you had the odd conversation with Andjelkovic. Am I correct I never had any communication with the -- with the staff of the Ministry of Interior in Pristina, anyone from that outfit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I think the only -- as I said, I told you we were picked up by the MUP in Djakovica and taken to the Glodjane massacre site.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. We'll get to -- I do have a couple questions with respect to Glodjane that we'll get to later in my questioning. Now, as far as the information you were relying upon regarding the activities of the MUP police in Kosovo and Metohija, can we conclude that apart from the items that you personally eyewitnessed in your statement that most of your other knowledge came primarily from other sources such as the KVM, KDOM, and the KLA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't think that's correct at all, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. What other sources did you rely upon then, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When it became obvious that the MUP were heavily involved in operations in Kosovo, I referred back to my own Ministry of Defence for intelligence in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But one keeps one's eye open. I had to brief the KVM, the KDOM. One spoke to members of the KLA, as I already admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. Did you ever attempt to hear the other side; that is to say, approach the high functionaries of the Serbian MUP to inquire about these activities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I've said, sir, there were times when I attempted to engage these gentlemen in conversation, and I put the questions through the FLS to be answered usually with not a great deal of interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that these gentlemen you attempted to engage in conversation are the gentlemen in Belgrade; that is to say, that the requests were made to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I think that that would be correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you've talked here in the last two days about your discussions with VJ Generals Dimitrijevic and Perisic and about the various comments that they made. The question I would like to ask you is as far as your discussions with these two individuals are concerned, did you note any tendency on their part to try and pass responsibility or shuffle responsibility from themselves onto the MUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I don't think that was the -- I think there was concern that I was noting -- there was some very harsh treatment being meted out, as I've already made clear during the last two days. And I'm sure that was passed on to the appropriate authorities, but that's about really all I can say on that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. If we can look at Exhibit P683 on e-court. This was an exhibit that was tendered by the Office of the Prosecutor, I believe through your -- through their presentation of you in this case the other day. And I'm looking at I believe page 4 on e-court paragraph 12. First of all, sir, looking at the first page of this document, does this appear to be a document that you had knowledge of or perhaps even authored during your deployment as the Defence attache to the UK embassy in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I may well have added to this document. I would have to read it. But as it's a DipTel, that comes from either my ambassador or the Deputy Head of Mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not authorised to release those, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did you say P683.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's what I'm showing, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's the one May Mr. Ackerman showed a short time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe it is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which the witness wasn't happy to comment on because it was a -- it contained views expressed by the ambassador.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's why I need to find out whether the comments that I'm referring to are comments the witness made or comments that the ambassador made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.
